d: A 3D flight-tracking globe in active development, with an early version live: a React and CesiumJS client over a static data pipeline, built to play back flights without an always-on server.
h: At a glance The problem Approach What I built What is planned What I’m learning Stack
b: AeroGlobe In active development · data pipeline & 3D visualization A browser-based 3D globe for flight tracking. It is a work in progress, and an early version is live. The implementation details and test counts below describe the 23 October 2026 snapshot, not a continuously updated release dashboard. Open the live site View the code Work in progress. This case study describes the code on 23 October 2026. The repository’s deployment notes⁠, checked on 6 November, still describe build-time OpenSky observations with a labeled sample-data fallback and a generated sample day. The live site⁠ is not a continuously polling live feed, and no real historical day is published yet. Dataset availability can change between builds. At a glance 282 test declarations in 43 files at the 30 October 2026 snapshot; not a current passing-test total 4 stages in the data pipeline: normalize, segment, chunk, catalog 8,090 lines of TypeScript at the same snapshot The problem Most flight trackers show what is in the air now. I wanted to look at flights that have already happened: where an aircraft went, how a route looked over a day, and what a busy hour of global traffic looks like on a globe. That is a data problem before it is a graphics problem. Bulk historical flight logs are large, free and awkward, and a live API gives you only a short window. My first version was live-first, polling an API every 15 seconds. Auditing it showed that a historical view needs a different shape: process the data ahead of time, publish it as static files, and let the browser do the rest. Approach AeroGlobe data flow as built so far: state vectors from short OpenSky samples, full adsb.lol days or generated fixtures pass through a Node pipeline that normalizes, segments into flights and chunks by hour, and writes a catalog and track files as static data; the React and CesiumJS client reads them, and a small Express proxy serves live polling in local development. The live site ships a short OpenSky sample recorded at build time and a labeled sample day; no real historical day is published yet. The client is React and TypeScript with CesiumJS for the globe. State lives in Zustand stores, and search and filtering work on a set derived from the flight store. A small Express server proxies the live feed for local development. The data side is a Node and TypeScript pipeline. It takes state vectors, turns them into per-aircraft tracks, splits each track into flights, slices the tracks into hourly chunks and writes a catalog. The output is plain JSON that a static host can serve, so there is no database and no always-on API. The pipeline puts a size limit on each hourly chunk and throws an error when a chunk goes over it. What I built The globe client. A Cesium viewer with aircraft markers, search, filters for region, altitude, status and airline, a flight detail card, a flight list and a dark and light skin. A static data pipeline. Normalization, flight segmentation, hourly chunking and a catalog, with a snapshot command that records a few OpenSky observations and a fixture command that writes a deterministic set of generated traces for offline work. A historical source. An adapter for full days of adsb.lol flight data, which runs through the same pipeline and can publish to a separate data branch from my own machine. A global day needs about 10 GB of disk. Playback and track replay. A day picker and a time slider with play and pause, driven by the globe’s clock, that moves every aircraft along its recorded positions. A Replay track control follows one selected aircraft, with an option to keep the camera on it. Up to 2,000 aircraft nearest the camera draw a short trail from their consecutive observations. Reference data. Airport and airline tables built from public sources, with the source and licence of each recorded next to the file, and time-zone polygons for the planned overlay. Tests and checks. The repository’s continuous integration runs lint, the type-checker, the tests and the build on pushes and pull requests to the main branch. What is planned The design spec for the next stage is a draft. In outline: a published historical day on the live site; a faster playback engine that decodes data off the main thread and draws aircraft as one layer, with a transport bar that sets the speed and shows traffic over the day; inferred routes between airports and a time-zone overlay; a per-aircraft history panel; a personal flight logbook kept in the browser. None of these is built yet beyond the basic playback above, and the spec may change as I build. What I’m learning Choose where the work happens before choosing the framework. Moving the heavy work into a build step is what makes a historical view possible without running a server. Fixtures are worth building early. Because the pipeline can run on generated traces, every stage has a test that needs no network. An audit of my own first version was more useful than adding features to it. Stack TypeScript React CesiumJS Zustand Vite Node Express Vitest

b: The Mandalay Bay: technical report Side project · game systems & simulation Open the terminal Walk the RPG Summary The Mandalay Bay is a satirical choose-your-adventure resort and casino simulator with one chip wallet. It runs as a Python command-line program, as a browser terminal and as a Phaser pixel-art overworld. The repository is named degen-llms as a joke. There is no language model in it. It is a systems project: one economy, three front ends, a save format that crosses them, and tests around the parts most likely to drift. It is satire. Chips are fictional, no real money is involved, and it is not affiliated with MGM Resorts International or the real Mandalay Bay. System and data Surfaces Surface Entry Role Python CLI python3 -m mandalay_bay Reference rules. Standard library only at runtime, Python 3.11 or later Browser terminal docs/index.html Hand-written vanilla JavaScript ES modules under docs/js/. Not Python compiled for the browser Pixel RPG docs/rpg/index.html Phaser overworld over the same modules By line count (wc, blank lines included) docs/js holds about 33k lines of JavaScript, and about 44k with docs/rpg/js added (the RPG layer is about 10k). The repository has about 27.4k lines of Python in all, including about 5.2k in tests and 6.8k in scripts. The runtime package itself is much smaller. Content as data Content Count Floors 8 Slot machines (slots_catalog.json) 37 Futures and options contracts 744 Sports scenarios 337 Prediction scenarios 204 Architecture The Mandalay Bay architecture: a Python CLI and a browser terminal each implement the rules; shared UI factories feed both the terminal and the Phaser RPG overlay; each surface reads and writes the same five-slot wallet schema, kept in the CLI's per-user directory or the browser's localStorage. The delegation rule. The RPG never reimplements a game screen. Casino, hotel, pool, shops, sportsbook, racing, cashier and the meta screens are each written once in docs/js/ui/ as a buildXRenderers(ctx) factory. It returns a map from view name to render function. The terminal spreads those maps into its RENDERERS table. The RPG’s TerminalHostOverlay builds the same ctx and mounts the same functions inside an encounter panel. Four screens are drawn by the RPG itself because they read better in the world: blackjack, hold’em, roulette and the House of Blues rhythm game. They still use the shared stake picker for bet entry. The architecture note adds a direction: new logic goes in docs/js/ first and the RPG consumes it, never the reverse. One wallet and the save format. A single ChipWallet is the source of truth. There are five save slots. The CLI keeps them in a per-user directory and the browser keeps a library in localStorage. They use the same schema but are not one live store, so a save moves between them only if someone copies it. The web save is version 8, and it carries an rpg block with map, position and flags. The CLI reads the version field tolerantly. The resort clock. world-cycle.js is the single clock for the resort. Two real hours equal one in-game day, which it divides into four named phases. Randomness The core table games and slots use a cryptographically secure generator. In Python that is a secrets.SystemRandom singleton, with Fisher–Yates shuffles for decks. In the browser the game modules draw from crypto.getRandomValues. A seeded generator is injected only in tests, so those tests are repeatable. One gap: the repository documentation says gameplay never uses Math.random, and that is not true. I grepped docs/js and docs/rpg/js and found 30 calls in 14 files. Several side-venue rolls that change chips or rewards still use it: the tip-back roll and amounts in the Gentleman’s Club (gentlemans-club.js), the bar encounter roll (bar.js), dining encounters (dining.js) and the pit top-up perk (rewards-perks.js). The arcade cabinets, the Strip Drive game and the rhythm overlay use it for spawns and sequences. The rest is cosmetic: dealer quips, message ids, effects and animation timing. The claim is wrong as written. Exact slot returns estimate_base_game_rtp in mandalay_bay/activities/slots.py does not simulate spins. It loops over every combination of symbols on the three reels. It multiplies the three symbol probabilities, runs the real payout function on that combination and sums probability times win. It returns the return to player and the hit frequency, excluding progressives. The result is exact, so a test can assert on it with no tolerance for sampling noise. The numbers are not realistic. A test named for the parody machine fortune pins its return between 155% and 185%, with a hit frequency of at least 28%. I also ran the estimator over all 37 machines in the catalog. Every one returns more than 100% in the base game: the lowest are fortune and high_roller at about 168%, and the highest is a salon machine at about 1,049%. Hit frequency ranges from about 4% to about 36%. These machines pay the player on average. That is the satire. Nothing here models real casino odds. Iteration history The changelog runs from 1.1.0 (2026-07-26) to 1.2.2 (2026-08-26). Merge history at the 30 October 2026 snapshot reaches the 160s, and the source changelog does not yet describe the later merges. I did not count commits. 1.1.0, 2026-07-26 — Trading Floor with 744 stored contracts, 337 sports events and 204 prediction scenarios, Arcade Alley cabinets, Vegas Strip Drive, craps and a lottery counter, and the walkable Strip overworld in the RPG. Rewards tier thresholds aligned to the docs: saves keep their lifetime totals and the tier is recomputed, so a player who had maxed the old ladder can drop until they wager more. Valet garage exit softlock fixed. 1.2.0, 2026-07-27 — Gentleman’s Club, resort dining and first-person bar overlays, the Mandalay Beach pool overlay, Strip Ride to away casinos, Rewards Phone audio and the Shoppes expansion. Fixes include the module cache bug, the slot redraw bug, tier gate syncing and a Strip Ride blank-screen crash (missing menuBtn helper). 1.2.1, 2026-07-27 — Distinct accent colours and table skins for the away-casino menus (Luxor, Excalibur, Bellagio, Circa), plus documentation parity. 1.2.2, 2026-08-26 — Python CLI parity for gambling, including text-mode Arcade Alley and the 37-machine slots catalog, and an Arcade Alley redeem shop whose perks feed the casino (a free-spin voucher, a welcome-drink refill). Fixes from a web-terminal casino audit (pending refunds on leave, in-flight slot and roulette spins) and from a pass over RPG hosted games and overlays, and a second menuBtn crash fix in the strip-limo screen. Bugs worth naming Module cache skew. The casino boot path loaded venues.js more than once because of ES-module cache skew, which duplicated its instances. The changelog lists it as fixed. I did not trace the fix itself. Slot redraw. The slot screen replaced the whole page every 90 ms while the reels spun, which glitched the spin. It now updates the reels in place. Valet garage softlock. The changelog describes a softlock when leaving the valet garage. It was fixed with wayfinding signs, path ramps and an interactive keys desk. Results There are no performance benchmarks. The evidence is the test suite, the CI run list and the screenshots below. Test counts These are collected, not pass rates. I did not run the suite for this report. Suite Count Source pytest 379 def test_ declarations at the 30 October 2026 snapshot grep over tests/; not a collected or passing count Node smoke scripts 12 scripts scripts/smoke-test-*.mjs Browser smoke test 1 script scripts/smoke-test-web.py CI (.github/workflows/checks.yml) runs pytest on Python 3.11. A second job runs on Node 22: a validation that every import under docs/js resolves, the browser smoke test, and all 18 Node scripts (13 smoke, 5 regression). tests/test_save_version_migration.py covers a version 3 save with no rewards state, version 7 tier fields, and a version 8 web save with an rpg block loading in the CLI. Figures The terminal front page with floor chips and a numbered menu. The table games menu. The slot machines menu. The sports book menu. These screenshots come from an earlier build. The slot screen’s text there (“nearly 1,000 reel games”) does not match the 37-machine catalog in the current data. Reproducibility python3 -m mandalay_bay # play the CLI python3 -m mandalay_bay --list-saves # list save slots python3 -m pytest # Python tests node scripts/validate-docs-imports.mjs # check browser module imports node scripts/smoke-test-rpg.mjs # RPG world data check The browser terminal is static files in docs/, so any static host can serve it. Playing cards in the games use the Kenney Playing Cards Pack (kenney.nl), released under CC0. Engineering quality Tests near the economy. Wallet, rewards, saves, hotel, sportsbook, lottery and slots each have their own test file. Import validation. A script walks the browser modules and fails if an import does not resolve. Tolerant saves. The CLI accepts newer web saves instead of refusing them. No runtime dependencies in Python. The package needs only the standard library. Limitations and next steps The README lags the code: it still says “200+ tests”, while the 30 October snapshot declares 379 pytest tests. The data files and the test tree are the authority. Package metadata says version 1.0.0 while the changelog is at 1.2.2. The Pages deploy is manual from the gh-pages branch, so the live demo can lag main. Blackjack rule tests are small: test_rules.py has 9 tests and test_hand.py has 8. Slot returns are parody numbers, not realistic odds. The Math.random calls in side-venue code (tips, bar, dining, rewards perk), described above, are a known gap against the project’s own claim. Python and the browser each implement the rules, so they can drift. The shared save schema and tests reduce that risk but do not remove it.

d: A satirical choose-your-adventure casino and resort simulator with one chip wallet, a Python CLI, a browser terminal and a pixel-art RPG that share their screens.
h: At a glance The problem Approach What I built Results What I learned Stack
b: The Mandalay Bay Side project · game systems & simulation The repository is called degen-llms. The name is tongue-in-cheek. There is no language model in it. Open the terminal Walk the RPG Satire only. Chips are fictional and nothing here uses real money. This project is not affiliated with MGM Resorts International or the real Mandalay Bay. At a glance 3 surfaces on one wallet: Python CLI, browser terminal, pixel RPG 379 + 18 pytest test declarations and Node smoke/regression scripts at the 30 October 2026 snapshot 744 futures and options contracts, among 37 slot machines and 8 floors The problem I wanted a game big enough to be a real software project: many small activities, one economy, and a save that survives. It is a resort where you pick a floor, play a game, spend chips on a room or a meal, and see the result on your balance. The joke is the setting. The work is keeping dozens of features consistent. Two things made it hard. The game has to run as a command-line program and in a browser. And a pixel-art overworld on top must not become a third copy of every screen. Approach The Mandalay Bay architecture: a Python CLI and a browser terminal each implement the rules; shared UI factories feed both the terminal and the Phaser RPG overlay; each surface reads and writes the same five-slot wallet schema, kept in the CLI's per-user directory or the browser's localStorage. The Python package is the reference for the rules and needs only the standard library, Python 3.11 or later. The browser terminal is a hand-written port in vanilla JavaScript ES modules. It is not Python compiled to run in the browser. The two sides share a save format, not a live store. The pixel RPG follows one rule: it never rebuilds a game screen. Each screen is written once as a factory, buildXRenderers(ctx), and both the terminal and the RPG overlay mount it. A feature added to the terminal shows up in the RPG with no RPG work. Four screens are the exception because they read better in the world: blackjack, hold’em, roulette and the House of Blues rhythm game. What I built One wallet. A single chip wallet is the source of truth. There are five save slots. The CLI saves to a per-user directory and the browser saves to localStorage. The web save is version 8, and a test loads a version 8 web save with RPG state in the CLI. Content. Eight floors, 37 slot machines, 337 sports scenarios, 204 prediction scenarios and 744 futures and options contracts, kept as data files. A resort clock. One clock module turns two real hours into one in-game day. Exact slot maths. The slot module can compute a machine’s return by listing every three-reel combination instead of simulating spins. Checks. CI runs pytest on Python 3.11. On Node 22 it runs a check that every browser module import resolves, the browser smoke test, and all 18 Node smoke and regression scripts. The earlier “7 of 12” description is superseded. Results The terminal’s front page: floor chips, the games on the floor today and a numbered menu. The table games menu: blackjack, Texas hold’em and roulette, each with a minimum bet. These captures come from an earlier build, when the front page listed five venues. The live demo has more. Heads up. The slot machines pay more than they take on purpose. A test pins one machine’s return between 155% and 185%, and exact enumeration over all 37 machines puts every one above 100% in the base game (about 168% at the low end). That is a satire economy, not realistic casino odds, and it should not be used to learn how real slots behave. What I learned Writing a screen once and mounting it in two hosts removed a whole class of drift between the terminal and the RPG. Computing slot returns by exact enumeration gave a number a test can pin, with no sampling noise. Two real bugs taught me the most: an ES-module cache mismatch loaded one file twice and made two copies of its state, and a slot screen redrew the whole page every 90 ms until I changed it to update the reels in place. Numbers written in a README go stale quickly. The changelog and the tests held up better. Stack Python JavaScript (ES modules) Phaser pytest Node GitHub Actions GitHub Pages

b: Digital-Mailroom DSHB capstone project · American Family Insurance (industry partner) At a glance 5 Python packages: entity extraction, classification, routing, scalable workflows 1 LangGraph pipeline joining routing, experiments, scoring, data and deployment Public data only the dataset was built from public sources; no partner data is involved Dec 2026 expected completion; results are not public yet The problem A mailroom takes in a stream of documents: contracts, merger agreements, corporate records, letters and emails, insurance claims. Someone, or something, has to read each one, decide what it is, pull out the key facts and send it to the right place. An LLM can do that, but running one on every page is expensive, and the cost grows with volume. The capstone with American Family Insurance asks how to cut the cost of AI inference while improving document processing. My part is the engineering behind that question: a pipeline that routes each document to the cheapest step that can handle it, and a way to measure whether the routing is any good. Approach The design is one LangGraph pipeline that joins legal-document routing, prompt experiments, deterministic scoring, dataset management and deployment in a single graph. The idea behind the cost goal is to send each document to the cheapest step that can handle it, and to reserve an LLM call for documents where that matters. The parts of Digital-Mailroom as the case study names them: the five components joined in one LangGraph pipeline, and the four areas the five Python packages cover. The diagram lists components; it does not show the order data moves through them. I split the work into five packages so each part can be tested and swapped on its own. What I built Five Python packages covering entity extraction, classification, routing and scalable workflows. One LangGraph pipeline that joins legal-document routing, prompt experiments, deterministic scoring, dataset management and deployment. Prompt experiments and deterministic scoring, so prompt choices are judged by fixed rules against known labels instead of by another model. Dataset management for the public-source dataset described below. A reproducible Docker environment so results can be rerun end to end. The dataset The capstone uses a dataset I assembled myself, called mailroom-dataset. It is built entirely from public datasets. None of the industry partner’s documents are in it, and none were used to build it. The versioned dataset citation and licensing notes identify the public corpus used in these studies. The public sources fall into three groups. Correspondence. The public Enron email corpus, deduplicated to unique texts, with labels from a mix of an LLM zero-shot pass, a join to a public email dataset, simple heuristics and manual review. Contracts, merger agreements and corporate records. Documents from public SEC filings. These include exhibits from EDGAR, and public contract, merger-agreement and registration-statement collections whose clause labels I mapped onto document types and subclasses. Insurance claims. b: Langton’s Ant Side project · simulation in the browser · version 0.1.0 A browser simulator for Langton’s ant and the wider family of two-dimensional Turing machines called turmites. I wrote the engine, the renderer and the interface. The mathematics of what these machines do comes from the literature listed at the bottom of this page, not from me. Open the simulator View the code At a glance 99 passing tests in 9 files, covering the engine, the permalink and session code, and the presets; a throughput benchmark is skipped unless asked for 20 preset machines in the gallery, each with its notation and a source 64 × 64 cells per grid chunk, one byte per cell, so 4 KiB a chunk The problem In 1986 Christopher Langton described an ant on a grid of cells. On a blank cell it turns right, paints the cell and steps forward; on a painted cell it turns left, clears the cell and steps forward. For about ten thousand steps the result looks like noise. Then the ant starts building a diagonal road that repeats every 104 steps and goes on forever. Whether this always happens is the open Highway Conjecture. Generalized ants, with more colors and more internal states, are called turmites, and some of them have been proved to be universal computers. The goal of the project is to run any of these machines in a browser, on a grid with no edge, deterministically, and to make a run something you can link to. Each of those three requirements shaped the code. Approach Langton's Ant structure: the app layer runs the animation loop, panels and permalinks and drives the renderer, which paints changed cells into an offscreen texture; both read the engine, which holds the rule tables, the chunked grid and the stepper. The engine has no browser dependency, so the same code runs under Vitest in Node. Everything runs on the main thread. The app is TypeScript built with Vite. It has no runtime dependencies, only development tools. The code is split into three folders. src/engine holds the rule tables, the grid and the stepper, and nothing in it touches the browser, so the same code runs in the page and under Vitest in Node. src/render paints the grid, and src/app runs the animation loop, the panels and the permalinks. A rule is one flat table indexed by state and color. For each pair it gives the color to write, the turn to make and the next state, so the classic ant is one state and two colors and a turmite is more of each. The engine accepts up to 32 colors and 16 states, in three notations: ant strings such as RL or LLRR, tables of triples in the style of the GollyGang Rule Table Repository, and decimal IDs. It refuses rule codes that would make an ant split in two, rather than guess at them. With more than one ant, every ant acts on every step, in array order. Engineering decisions Chunked typed arrays, not a sparse map. The grid is a map from chunk coordinates to 64 × 64 Uint8Array chunks, created the first time a cell in them is written. Chunk coordinates are packed into one number so that long highways do not collide. The repository’s memory comparison⁠ now reports one 20-million-step run per rule: a per-cell map used about 32× the chunk bytes for RLR, 34× for LLRR and 6× for the classic ant. These are pattern-specific measurements, not a universal memory ratio. One thread, on purpose. Sharing memory with a worker needs the COOP and COEP response headers, and GitHub Pages cannot send them. So the simulation runs on the main thread, and the code contains no worker. Repaint only what changed. Every step records the cell it wrote. The renderer keeps an offscreen texture at one pixel per cell and updates only those cells: one small write per cell up to 512 changes in a frame, and above that a repaint of the touched chunks with buffers that are reused rather than reallocated. The visible canvas then gets one scaled draw of the texture. The grid is unbounded, but the texture is capped at about 16.7 million pixels; past that it re-centers on recent activity. Determinism you can test. The step function is integer-only, and the engine never calls Math.random. The one source of randomness, placing stray ants, goes through a seeded generator (mulberry32). A single test runs the classic ant for 11,000 steps from a blank grid and compares an FNV-1a hash of the visited region with a committed value, 6219b3fb. That one assertion covers integer stepping, chunk addressing across negative coordinates, and the rule table. Permalinks in the URL hash. The hash carries the rule, the ants, the step count, the camera, the palette and the seed (#r=…&a=…&i=…&s=…&z=…&c=…&x=…). It never goes to a server. When the run-length encoding of the grid is at most 900 characters, the grid rides along too. What I built The engine. Rule parsers and encoders for the three notations, the chunked grid, the stepper, the PRNG and the hash. The renderer and interface. A Canvas2D renderer with pan and zoom, a rule editor, palettes, a dark and a light theme, keyboard shortcuts, PNG and WebM export, and session export as JSON. A preset gallery. Twenty machines, each with its notation, a one-line milestone where one is known and a link to its source: the classic ant, ants with three to twelve colors, ants whose highways have been proved, two turmites that stay chaotic for millions of steps, halting machines and absolute-heading turmites. Tests. Ninety-nine Vitest tests across the rule parsers, the grid, the simulation, serialization, the highway detector, session restore, the preset gallery and the golden hash, and a type-check that passes. Results The classic ant (rule RL) at step 15,181, with the grid readout in the top bar. The irregular cluster is the first ten thousand or so steps. The road is the highway. The 24.0 KB in the top bar is six 4 KiB chunks. A replay of the classic ant without a browser checks its numbers: it settles into a 104-step cycle that moves it two cells along each axis, from about step 9,976, which matches the figure of about 9,977 steps in the gallery’s milestone. The repository’s README reports how fast the engine steps in Node. Those numbers come from one laptop. The same benchmark re-run on a different machine shows how much they depend on it. Steps per second: README laptop against three re-runs (millions) Re-runs (shared Linux container) README (Apple M2 laptop) Engine throughput in Node, with no browser and no rendering. The benchmark logs its timings and asserts nothing, so throughput never fails a test. These are not browser frame rates, which have not been measured. 1,000,000 steps per run, mean of 5 README: Apple M2, macOS, Node 22.14.0 Re-runs: shared 4-core Linux container, Node 22.22.0 Classic RL ant, one ant 19.65 million steps per second 4.28, 10.63 and 13.18 million in three re-runs Colony of 25 ants 0.54 million steps per second, 13.39 million cell updates per second 0.19, 0.29 and 0.31 million in three re-runs The throughput depends heavily on the machine, and it varied by a factor of three between runs on the same shared container, so treat the README’s figures as one laptop’s result. The determinism test does not depend on the machine: the 11,000-step hash also passes on the Linux re-run. Where the mathematics comes from None of the following is my work. They are the papers this project’s README cites for its claims. Langton, C. G., “Studying artificial life with cellular automata,” Physica D 22 (1986): the original paper⁠. Gajardo, Moreira and Goles, “Complexity of Langton’s ant,” Discrete Applied Mathematics 117 (2002): arXiv⁠. Gajardo, Hellouin de Menibus, Maldonado and Moreira, “Nontrivial Turmites Are Turing-Universal” (2017): arXiv⁠. Gajardo, Lutfalla and Rao, “Ants on the highway,” Natural Computing (2025): arXiv⁠. Lutfalla, “Sideways on the highways” (2025): arXiv⁠, and “The LLLR generalised Langton’s ant” (2025): arXiv⁠. b: MORNINGSTAR: technical report LLM agent design · prompt architecture Summary MORNINGSTAR is a deliberative persona framework in the repository LLM_Personas. It runs decisions about architecture, implementation and debugging as courtroom proceedings: a triage step, a cast with fixed roles, arguments, a rule-bound vote and a written ruling. It is mostly prompt and persona markdown, about 54,000 lines, plus a Python layer of about 5,700 lines. The version is 0.0.4. The package metadata says “Internal use”, and the repository has no licence file, so it is not open source in the usual sense. One point matters more than the rest. The runner makes one model call that plays every seat. It is not a multi-model system. There is also no evaluation: no baseline and no comparison with a single prompt. This report describes the design and the evidence that it runs, and it publishes no quality claim. System and data The cast and the rules Role Votes Notes Judge tie-break only Presides, seats specialists, casts the deciding vote with an explanation Architect, Engineer, Debugger, Prophet, Counsel 1 each The five standard voters, cast in that order Scribe 0 Records decisions and maintains state Non-voting consultant persona 0 Advisory, invoked by the judge Witnesses 0 Expert domains called with /summon <domain>-expert Specialists 1 each Seated by the judge only, F3 and above, up to 2 at a time Spectators 0 Optional commentary; they do not deliberate, testify or vote A valid deliberation needs the judge, at least 3 voting members including the Prophet, and the scribe. There are 27 expert domains in courtroom/domains/experts.yaml (25 can be called as witnesses or seated as specialists; 2 are advisory only), each with a scope, heuristics, signature questions and a stated failure mode. Feasibility triage. Matters are rated F0 to F5. F3 and above must be deliberated, F4 requires a transcript and F5 a full record. There are four proceeding types: standard, expedited, special-interest hearing (testimony and findings, no final vote) and contempt hearing. One inconsistency: courtroom/RULES.md names F0 “Trivial”, while core/MFAF.md names it “Infrastructural”, a currently impossible idea that reveals a missing capability. Voting. A yes vote counts +1, no counts -1, abstain 0, and a recused member is excluded. A motion passes if yes votes exceed no votes. Votes are cast in a canonical order, and the tally must match the individual votes. When votes are tied, the rules say the Prophet loses first, then specialists lose by recency of seating (most recent first), and the judge breaks any remaining tie. The ruling has five parts: Decision, Vote, Rationale, Risk and Dissent. Commands. /morningstar, /update and /end open, checkpoint and close a session. /aegis calls a security-focused agent. /summon <domain>-expert, /seat <domain>-specialist, /dismiss, /sme status and /sme domains manage experts. Two ways to run it First, five Cursor agent definitions in .cursor/agents/ (four are also under agents/), where the model reads the persona files and follows the procedure over a conversation. Second, litigation/run.py. It loads a summary of session state, builds a system prompt and a user prompt from the framework files, and calls provider.complete once (around lines 277 to 297). The response is the whole transcript: arguments, vote and ruling, all written by one model. This is a design choice. It keeps cost low and works with small local models. The limitation is that the personas are not independent. A vote among them is one model agreeing or disagreeing with itself. The prompt assembler has nine include_* toggles (best practices, checklists, domain experts, MFAF, personalities, procedures, rules, spectators and templates) to cut context size. The runner caps max_tokens at 32,768. Providers sit behind a base class and a factory: Ollama, LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible server, and OpenRouter. The CLI offers the four proceeding types as standard, expedited, special_inquiry and contempt. What the prompt contains The system prompt is assembled from the framework files: procedures, rules, personalities, checklists, the expert registry, the feasibility framework and optionally spectators and templates. A short runner instruction tells the model to produce a complete transcript with all phases and to end with scribe certification. The user prompt carries the matter, the feasibility level, the hearing type and a state summary. The model is told to follow the procedure. Nothing in code checks that it did, apart from the separate transcript audit described below. Records and state Item What it does state/current.md Session state, validated against core/state-schema.md Case IDs 2026-DEL-005-001 style: year, category, case number, deliberation number courtroom/case-registry.yaml Holds the next case number per category; allocate_case_no in run.py increments it courtroom/reporter.py Audits transcript names and headers, regenerates the portal manifest, prints an integration report Court Reporter agent Acts on that report: updates courtroom/precedents.md and state/metrics.md The executive layer The executive/ package has four standard-library modules, about 600 lines in all. By design it executes rulings and does not make decisions. Module Behaviour judicial_log.py Append-only log. Each entry carries a SHA-256 entry hash and the previous entry’s hash, and verify() walks the chain proof.py HMAC-SHA256 proof over ruling ID, reason and timestamp, required to override a ruling. The secret file is gitignored watchdog.py Flags actions with no logged approval and no override proof, log integrity failures, and more than 5 overrides consensus.py File-based proposal, vote, quorum (default 3 of 5) and commit I found no call from litigation/run.py into this package. The executive layer is a library with tests, not yet a step in the runner. Web interface index.html is a live UI. It stores an OpenRouter key in the browser’s localStorage, which is convenient and exposes the key to anything running on that page. backend/server.js is an Express proxy that keeps the key in a server environment variable instead. The two are alternatives, and the trade-off is real. Iteration history The changelog runs from 2026-02-15 to 2026-07-25. The changelog and metrics file are my evidence; I did not use commit history, because the clone I read has a single commit. 2026-02-15 — Infrastructure, a framework enhancement analysis (which added the state validation schema), a spectators file and an Aegis security subagent. 2026-02-17 — The expert registry grew by 15 domains, to 27, after a bench trial on the question. 2026-02-19 — A case naming and numbering format, and an executive branch with a log, override proofs, a watchdog and a consensus protocol. 2026-07-25 — A docket of four proceedings: agentic production mutation controls, open-weight model export controls, agent-authored legal filings and agentic cyber attribution. The last was a special-interest hearing, so it produced findings and no vote. Results There are no benchmark or quality results. The evidence is the record the system produced and the Python tests. What the project reports about itself state/metrics.md says 13 deliberations, 12 decisions, 8 unanimous and 3 split, with 0 tie-breakers and 0 deadlocks. The feasibility counts are 2 at F3, 4 at F4 and 7 at F5. These come from the same system that produced the decisions and I did not recompute them. The vote categories add up to 11 rather than the 12 decisions it reports, so the file is not fully consistent with itself. The 8 unanimous votes are a weak signal when one model casts all the votes. Test counts Suite Count Where pytest collection 62 tests tests/ Test functions by grep 59 def test_ in 13 files tests/test_*.py The two numbers differ because parametrised tests expand at collection. I ran collection only. I did not run the suite, so I make no pass-rate claim. The files cover the judicial log, override proof, watchdog, consensus, prompt assembler, runner, transcript viewers and court reporter. Reproducibility python litigation/run.py "Should we adopt a new naming convention for API endpoints?" python litigation/viewer.py list python -m pytest A run needs a provider: a local Ollama or LM Studio server, or an OpenRouter key. Output varies between runs: the example config sets temperature to 0.7, and hosted models change over time. Nothing here is deterministic the way a simulation is. Python 3.9 or later is required. Engineering quality Rules in the open. Voting, tie-breaking and ruling format are written down in courtroom/RULES.md, and the vote must match the tally. Tamper evidence. The judicial log detects edits and reordering. Like any chain on one disk, it cannot show that the tail was cut off. Secrets. The override secret is gitignored, and the proxy keeps the API key server-side. Context control. The include toggles and the token cap let small models run the framework. Limitations and next steps One model, one vote. The runner’s court is a single model. Unanimity is a weak signal, and the stated disagreements are performed. No evaluation. There is no baseline and no comparison with a plain prompt. Self-reported metrics. The dashboard is maintained by the system it measures. Overdue review. state/current.md marks the F4+ specialist pilot review, due 2026-05-18, as overdue. A model-list bug. In litigation/models.py, several entries in the free-model list lack a trailing comma, so Python joins neighbouring strings into single, invalid model IDs. Licence. There is no open-source licence. Executive layer not wired in. The runner does not write to the judicial log. Prompt compliance is unchecked. The runner does not parse the transcript to confirm the vote matches the tally or that all five ruling parts are present. Proposed evaluation (future work, not done) Fix a set of 30 or more past engineering decisions with a known outcome or an expert-agreed good answer. For each, get two answers: one from MORNINGSTAR, one from a single plain prompt with the same model and a similar token budget. Have raters who do not know which is which score both on correctness, risk coverage and usefulness of the dissent. Compare the pairs, and test whether separate calls per persona beat the single-call court.

b: MORNINGSTAR LLM agent design · prompt architecture The repository is called LLM_Personas. MORNINGSTAR is the name of the court inside it. At a glance 5 voting personas, plus a judge who breaks ties and a scribe who records 27 expert domains (25 can also be seated as specialists; 2 are advisory only) 62 tests collected by pytest for the Python layer; I did not run them The problem When I ask a model to choose between two designs, I usually get a smooth answer that agrees with whatever I leaned toward. I wanted a way to make it argue first. I also wanted the decision to leave a record: who said what, how the vote went, what the risk is, and who disagreed. MORNINGSTAR is my attempt. A decision about architecture, implementation or debugging is run as a courtroom proceeding with fixed roles, fixed voting rules and a fixed ruling format. Approach The MORNINGSTAR flow: a matter is triaged on a feasibility scale, the cast argues and votes, and the ruling goes into a transcript that the runner writes to a file. In the runner, one model call plays every seat in the cast. The executive layer, with its hash-chained log and watchdog, is drawn dashed and detached because it is a separate, tested library that the runner does not call yet. A matter is first rated for feasibility, from F0 to F5. F3 and above must be deliberated. F4 requires a transcript and F5 a full record. The court has a judge who votes only to break a tie, five voting personas (Architect, Engineer, Debugger, Prophet and Counsel), a scribe who records and does not vote, and a non-voting consultant persona. Witnesses can be called in with zero votes. For F3 and above the judge may seat specialists with one vote each. Each persona argues in turn. Votes are cast in a fixed order, a vote of yes counts +1 and no counts -1, and a motion passes if yes votes exceed no votes. The ruling has five parts: Decision, Vote, Rationale, Risk and Dissent. Heads up. In the runner, one model plays the whole court. litigation/run.py builds one large prompt and makes one completion call. The judge, the five voters and the scribe are all the same model, in the same pass. This is not a swarm of separate models. I chose it because it is cheap and simple, but it limits what the vote can tell you. What I built Personas as files. Most of the repository, about 54,000 lines, is markdown: personas, rules, checklists and templates. About 5,700 lines are Python. Two ways to use it. Five Cursor agent definitions in .cursor/agents/ (four are also under agents/), driven by commands such as /morningstar, /summon <domain>-expert and /seat <domain>-specialist. Or a command-line runner that works with Ollama, LM Studio or OpenRouter. Four proceeding types. Standard, expedited, special-interest hearing (findings only, no vote) and contempt hearing. A record. Case IDs look like 2026-DEL-005-001 (year, category, case number, deliberation number), with the next number kept in a registry file. Session state is a markdown file checked against a written schema. An executive layer, not wired in. A library with tests: a hash-chained, append-only log of rulings, HMAC proofs for overrides, a watchdog that checks actions against approvals, and a small file-based quorum vote. The runner does not call it yet, so its transcripts are not written to the hash-chained log. Context controls. The prompt assembler has nine include toggles, and the runner caps the response length, so a small local model can still take part. A browser UI and a proxy. index.html is a live UI. backend/server.js is an Express proxy that keeps the API key on the server. Results There are no results to report. I have never compared MORNINGSTAR with a single plain prompt, so I cannot say it gives better decisions. It is a design exploration. What I can say is what it produced. The project’s own metrics file reports 13 deliberations and 12 decisions: 8 unanimous, 3 split and no tie-breakers. Those categories add up to 11, not 12, so the file is not fully consistent with itself. A set of July 2026 rulings covered controls for agents that change production systems, export controls on open-weight models, agent-authored legal filings and attribution of agentic cyber attacks. Those numbers are self-reported by the same system, and unanimity from one model voting with itself is a weak signal. I have not added screenshots, because there is no interface worth showing in a still. What I learned A written ruling format forces the model to state a risk and a dissent. That is useful even when the vote is not. Most of the value I can see is in the structure and the record, not in the vote. Saying “one model, one call” plainly changes how much weight the unanimous votes deserve. A design with no baseline is easy to like and hard to defend. The next step is a paired comparison, described in the report. Stack Markdown Python YAML Ollama LM Studio OpenRouter Node.js Express pytest

Data engineering · dataset build, audit & publishing View the code Dataset on Hugging Face Summary Mailroom-Corpus-EDA is the audit and publishing repository for the mailroom dataset, a corpus of 3,302 legal and insurance documents in five classes and 55 strata. The repository downloads the published dataset, checks its structure and provenance, measures its composition, draws 30 static and 18 interactive figures, audits correspondence intent coverage, and holds the helpers that build and publish new revisions to the Hugging Face Hub. This report describes the Hub tag v9.2. The current published revision is v9.3, released in November 2026: it adds corporate presence-layer labels over the same 3,302 documents and routes merger agreements to their own specialist. A v9.4 revision is staged and not yet published. It is an evaluation and ingress-simulation corpus for the mailroom projects. It is not a training set, and the report says where that matters. System and data Sources Class Documents Source Licence insurance_claim 1,100 CMS DE-SynPUF, GNOTHEIA, a motor-claims decision set, INSURBIAS Apache-2.0, MIT or CC BY 4.0, depending on the source correspondence 1,000 Enron email, deduplicated (a pool of 247,523 rows) Research use; real named individuals, so handled conservatively contract 600 CUAD v1 (509) and SEC EDGAR exhibits (91) CC BY 4.0 and US public domain corporate_record 450 SEC EDGAR filing exhibits US public domain merger_agreement 152 MAUD v1 CC BY 4.0 I excluded three candidate insurance samples because they carry a non-commercial licence. No label column ground_truth 3,302 Labels in a gt_fields JSON column, identity and hashes, the evaluation contract, matter and group fields: 35 top-level columns and a 34-key gt_fields union bundles 50 Synthetic multi-document families built over real anchor documents, flagged as constructed streams 62 One interleaved ingress stream with distractor documents fixtures 32 Recovery and adversarial fixtures Pipeline Phase What it does Output P0 Download the dataset snapshot and validate its manifest data/parquet/ (git-ignored) P1 Structural integrity and provenance audit reports/tables/integrity_report.json P2 Composition: strata, imbalance, provenance, metadata coverage strata and imbalance tables P3 Static figures and tables 30 PNGs P4 Interactive figures 18 Plotly HTML files P5 Cast-safe JSONL and parquet staging helpers data/staging/ P6 Correspondence intent coverage and provenance audit reports/SUMMARY_REPORT.json run_all.py runs all seven phases, or any subset with --phases. The summary JSON is written only by a full run, because a subset run once overwrote the full-corpus summary with partial numbers. The src/mailroom_eda/ package is about 21,100 lines of Python at the 6 November 2026 snapshot (revision 32d34a2). Its modules cover identity, the evaluation contract, matter grouping, the integrity audit, ground-truth quality rules, the intent backfill, token budgets, export and the Hub client. Method Label separation The blind configuration is the surface a model sees, so nothing derived from a label may appear on it. An early revision still carried two integers in the blind metadata, a contract clause count and a merger annotation count. Both are functions of the hidden labels and leak a weak signal: a non-zero count says the document has labelled clauses. The v9.1 revision moved them into the ground-truth configuration. The hardened release code never restages the blind configuration, so labels cannot ride along with it. Identity and provenance A document id is derived from the source corpus and source filename. It does not come from a row index, the content, the split or the configuration, so it survives rebuilds and reordering. Two rows may share content, since duplicates are a legitimate mailroom scenario, but each row stays a distinct incoming artefact. Content and normalised-text SHA-256 hashes support duplicate detection and rebuild verification. The published annotation_method records six regimes for how a label was produced: Regime Rows source_native 661 heuristic 646 llm_zero_shot 637 synthetic 1,100 verified_join 162 human_annotated 96 The six counts add up to 3,302, one regime per row. Correspondence intent The canonical vocabulary is eight classes: analysis, meeting_invite, notice, other, payment_demand, press_communication, request and update. other is the explicit fallback, never null. Rows reach a label by one of four disjoint paths, recorded in intent_source: Path Rows Exact-body join against a larger Enron corpus and AESLC, by SHA-256 of the normalised, header-stripped body 162 Subject-line heuristic 105 Constrained zero-shot model pass 637 Manual 96 All 1,000 correspondence rows have an intent, and 25 are flagged for review. The model pass is checkpointed, so a rerun skips rows that already have a label. Split rule and determinism A document goes to the test set when the MD5 of its filename modulo 10 is zero. That gives 2,979 train and 323 test rows, stable across rebuilds. Random state is fixed at 42, rows are sorted before export, and a rebuild of the JSONL and parquet files is byte-identical. The interactive Plotly figures are the one exception, because each embeds a random identifier, so the committed files are treated as canonical. Test share for each of the 55 strata, against the 10% the split rule aims for. Export hardening Metadata keys are uniform and string-typed, and absence is an empty string. JSON Lines output escapes the Unicode line separators (U+2028, U+2029 and NEL), because some readers split records on them. A verification script compares a local export byte for byte against the Hub. Results Integrity The blind and ground-truth configurations agree on all 3,302 filenames. The split rule has zero mismatches. All 13,753 CUAD span annotations match the document text at their stated character offsets. The MAUD annotation count matches the count in the labels for all 152 merger agreements. Composition The largest class is 7.2 times the smallest, and the largest stratum is 557 times the smallest. One merger-agreement stratum, a mixed cash and stock election, has a single document. Ten strata have no test document and five have fewer than ten documents in total. Documents per class on the left; distinct subclasses per class on the right. Text and token geometry Token counts use a characters-divided-by-four heuristic. Share of documents that fit each context window Context window Documents that fit 4,096 76.6% 16,384 89.6% 32,768 93.2% 65,536 95.0% 131,072 99.8% Merger agreements are the long tail, with a mean near 22,000 tokens and a maximum near 63,000. Insurance claims are short, about 690 characters on average. Revision history Revision Rows What changed v8 (frozen baseline) 2,000 The starting corpus, kept pinned and never deleted v9 3,302 Added 650 correspondence, 411 corporate records, 91 contracts and 150 insurance claims v9.1 3,302 Moved label-derived counts out of the blind metadata, added a per-row presence code for every label field, and added context-window bands v9.2 3,302 Published all six provenance regimes, removed an undocumented build-internal column, filled in relation fields on 23 heuristic rows, and corrected one audit v9.3 3,302 Label-only: built on the corporate relabel published as corporate-labels-v9.2.1, added presence codes for corporate entity fields, and routed the 152 merger agreements to merger_agreement_specialist None of v9.1, v9.2 or v9.3 added or removed a document, or changed an identifier or any document text. The changelog records zero drift. The tables and counts in this report and its appendix are for v9.2. An audit that was wrong After the v9.1 change moved the MAUD count to the ground-truth side, the integrity audit kept reading it from the blind metadata. It regenerated its report without error and printed a count-consistency result of 0 of 152. Nothing was wrong with the data. The audit was looking in the old place. The v9.2 revision reads the ground-truth count, restores the correct 152 of 152, and pins the case with a regression test. Tests I ran the test suite in a fresh environment, with the latest versions of the dependencies and not the pinned ones. That older run had 200 tests, of which 185 passed, 14 skipped and 1 failed. The current revision declares 594 def test_ functions in 26 files; that is a count, not a passing run. The 14 skipped tests need the full dataset snapshot, which run_all.py --phases P0 downloads. The 14 skipped tests need the full dataset snapshot, which run_all.py --phases P0 downloads. The failure is a contract test that reads a taxonomy file from a sibling checkout of another repository, which my environment did not have. Limitations Evaluation corpus, not a training set. The 90/10 split is for reproducible sampling and is not stratified, so ten strata have no test documents. Imbalance. The largest stratum is 557 times the smallest, so any per-stratum score is noisy for the small ones. No clause annotations on 91 contracts. The SEC EDGAR exhibits were never annotated. Provenance mix. 637 intents come from a zero-shot model pass and 1,100 insurance labels are synthetic, so results on those rows describe the labelling method as much as the documents. Personal data. The Enron emails are real messages from named people. Token counts are a heuristic. Characters divided by four will differ from a real tokenizer. Continuous integration is a placeholder. The repository’s own workflow prints a message and does not run the tests, so a regression would not be caught automatically. d: The data engineering behind the mailroom dataset: 3,302 documents assembled from public sources, with identity, provenance, label separation and an audit pipeline that checks every number it publishes.
h: At a glance The problem Approach What I built Results What I learned Cite the dataset Stack
b: Mailroom-Corpus-EDA Data engineering · dataset build, audit & publishing The mailroom projects all depend on one dataset. This repository is how I built it from public sources, cleaned it, checked it, and published it without letting the labels leak. View the code Dataset on Hugging Face At a glance 3,302 documents in 5 classes and 55 strata, from CUAD, MAUD, SEC EDGAR, Enron email and four insurance sources 13,753 of 13,753 contract clause annotations whose character offsets match the document text exactly 7 pipeline phases, from download to a correspondence-intent audit, rerun with one command The problem I could not find a public dataset that looks like a mailroom: contracts, merger agreements, corporate filings, emails and insurance claims arriving together. The only way to get one was to assemble it from sources that were never meant to sit side by side. They differ in format, licence, labelling, length and quality. Assembling the pieces is the smaller job. The harder part is being able to say, for every document, where it came from, what its label means, who produced the label, and whether a model scored on it could have seen the answer. Approach Mailroom-Corpus-EDA data flow: public sources are built into the mailroom dataset with stable identifiers and provenance; the dataset is published with the labels in a separate configuration from the blind documents; the audit pipeline downloads the published data back from the Hub and writes figures, tables and a summary report. The dataset is built once from public sources, and then the repository audits the published result. Every phase works from the published data, downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub, and recomputes its numbers, so the report is a check on the dataset and not a description of it. The design rule that shaped the most work is label separation. The main configuration a model reads has four columns: a filename, the document text, a prompt and a metadata blob. It has no label column. All ground truth lives in a second configuration that is joined on filename. A model working on the first configuration cannot see an expected class, an intent or a clause annotation. What I built Sources, with licences tracked. Contracts from CUAD and SEC EDGAR exhibits, merger agreements from MAUD, corporate records from EDGAR filings, correspondence from a deduplicated Enron corpus, and insurance claims from four sources, which are all recorded as synthetic. I left out three candidate insurance samples because they carry a non-commercial licence. Identity and provenance. Each row has a stable document id, derived from its source and filename and not from its row position, plus content hashes. A rebuild changes none of them. Each label also records how it was produced: a verified join, a model, a person, a heuristic, source-native, or synthetic. Fixing correspondence intent. Many email rows had no intent label. I hydrated them by an exact match on a hash of the normalised body against a larger Enron corpus and against AESLC, ran a constrained model pass on the rest, and recorded which path produced each label. All 1,000 rows now have one of eight intents. Hardened export. The exporter keeps metadata types uniform and handles the Unicode line separators that break JSON Lines readers. A byte-verify script compares a local export against what is on the Hub. An audit pipeline. Integrity, composition, 30 static figures, 18 interactive figures, 17 tables, and a summary report, all rerunnable. Tests. 594 def test_ declarations in 26 files at the 6 November 2026 snapshot cover identity, the integrity audit, ground-truth quality rules, fixtures and the revision builders. They are counted, not run. Results Documents per class on the left; distinct subclasses per class on the right. The corpus is imbalanced, and the audit says so plainly. The largest class is 7.2 times the smallest. At the level of the 55 strata the ratio is 557, because one merger-agreement stratum has a single document. The split rule puts a document in the test set when the md5 of its filename modulo 10 is zero, which is reproducible but not stratified. Ten strata end up with no test documents. Test share for each of the 55 strata, against the 10% the split rule aims for. Heads up. The dataset is built for evaluating a mailroom pipeline. It is not a training set, and its 90/10 split is a way to sample reproducibly, not a train and test design. The 91 SEC EDGAR contracts have no clause annotations. The Enron emails are real messages from named people, so I handle them conservatively, and any use of them should too. What I learned Once a dataset has several sources, provenance is part of the data. Recording how each label was made turned “this is 100% filled” into a claim I could check. A published report can be wrong without anything crashing. After I moved a count out of the blind metadata to stop it leaking, the audit kept reading the old location and reported 0 of 152 consistent. It had been checking the wrong place, not finding a bug in the data. I fixed the audit and added a test. Deterministic builds pay for themselves. Because a rebuild gives the same bytes, a change that should not touch any row is something I can prove, not something I hope. Public sources need unglamorous work: checking licences, handling odd characters, and writing down the known gaps instead of hiding them. Cite the dataset mailroom-dataset (revision v9.2) [Data set]. Hugging Face, repository Lucius-Morningstar/mailroom-dataset. Versioned dataset and card⁠. Accessed 6 November 2026. This is a repository citation, not a claim of a peer-reviewed publication or a DOI. Record the revision and configuration used (default or ground_truth) when reproducing results. The dataset card records the component sources and their separate license and attribution requirements; citing the combined corpus does not replace those obligations. b: Mailroom-ML: technical report ModernBERT ingest classifier · training, calibration, routing Historical report through M9b. “Final run” on this page means the four-epoch M9b run in this original comparison, not the current model release. The later M9c release has different accuracy, calibration, routing and release-gate results; see the updated case study. The tables and figures below retain their original experiment scope. Summary Mailroom-ML trains a hierarchical ModernBERT-base classifier for legal and insurance documents. It has one document-type head and one subclass head per type. Its job is to give a calibrated answer and a routing decision: either “this is safe to accept” or “send it to the LLM sorter”. On the final run, scored on the 323-document test split (541 windows), document-type accuracy is 0.9505 and window ECE is 0.0152. Under the routing gate, 74.3% of documents take the fast path, meaning they are handled without an LLM call. The fast-path and coverage numbers are optimistic, because the sweep that supports the 0.97 routing cutoff and the decode sweep both ran on this same split (see Routing and selective risk). Three of four acceptance gates are met. Contract subclass F1 is 0.162 against a floor of 0.20, so the subclass heads are not ready to act without the LLM. Numbers on this page labelled “test split” come from those 323 documents. The split was kept out of training, out of checkpoint selection (done on validation) and out of calibration fitting. It is not untouched, though. I used it to compare runs, to run the selective-risk sweep that supports the 0.97 cutoff, and to run the decode sweep. The 0.97 value itself is a preset in the project’s config, and the sweep recommended the same value. I name the project’s runs as follows: Run 3 is an early two-epoch run, Arm A and Arm B are two comparison runs (a one-epoch smoke run and a three-epoch run), and M9b is the final four-epoch run. The six figures are from Arm B, not from the final run. Where the two differ I say so. System and data Stages and modules Stage What it does Module Configuration One file holds the pinned data revisions, taxonomy, window sizes and routing thresholds that every other module imports src/mailroom_ml/config.py Normalisation A deterministic text clerk that runs before training and before inference, so the two see the same bytes src/mailroom_ml/normalize.py Windowing Token-level windows of 8,192 tokens with 512 tokens of overlap, plurality vote across windows src/mailroom_ml/windows.py Dataset build Stages the training set, splits it, and runs the leak audits src/mailroom_ml/dataset.py Provenance sha256 helpers and a byte-deterministic build manifest src/mailroom_ml/provenance.py Training PyTorch training with checkpoint selection on validation training/train/train_modernbert.py Calibration Per-head temperature scaling, ECE, Wilson bounds, selective-risk sweep src/mailroom_ml/calibration.py Out-of-distribution Energy probe on the document-type logits, fit on validation src/mailroom_ml/ood.py Routing Fast-path gate over calibrated confidence, agreement and margin src/mailroom_ml/routing.py Evaluation Test-split scoring, cohorts, selective risk, paired bootstrap comparison training/eval/eval_modernbert.py, training/eval/compare_runs.py Deployment ONNX export, parity check, Modal train and serve apps deploy/onnx_export.py, deploy/onnx_parity_check.py, deploy/modal_app.py, deploy/serve_app.py Data The corpus has 3,302 documents in 55 document-type by subclass strata. The test split holds 323 of them, and the other 2,979 are split 90/10 into train and validation (2,680 and 299 documents; 5,068 windows in total). Splits are stratified by document type with a fixed seed. There are five trained document types: contract, merger agreement, corporate record, correspondence and insurance claim. A sixth label, unknown, exists only at inference as an abstention. The corpus was built from public sources; the Digital-Mailroom case study describes how. The test split contains 60 contracts, 47 corporate records, 85 pieces of correspondence, 114 insurance claims and 17 merger agreements. Several subclass cells have only a handful of examples, which limits what the subclass numbers can show. Data lineage Every source in the build is pinned to an exact revision, never a floating tip. The build manifest records the source revision, split rule, label-normalisation rules, and leak-audit counts. It contains no timestamps, so rebuilding from the same inputs gives the same bytes, and the publish step checks each file’s sha256 against what was uploaded. A test module covers the provenance code. Iteration history Run 3 — Two epochs, class weights, leak-fixed and clerk-normalised data. Test-split document-type accuracy 0.8947, window ECE 0.0203. Contract and correspondence heads close to useless. Arm A — One epoch with document-type loss weight 0.50, a short smoke run. Accuracy 0.8638; under-trained. Arm B — Three epochs, document-type loss weight 0.65. Accuracy 0.9505, window ECE 0.0259, subclass accuracy given a correct type 0.5831. Chosen as the candidate release. No setting reached 0.20, so no retrain on that recipe. The adjustment did lift the other heads: merger-agreement F1 rose from 0 to about 0.16 and correspondence F1 from 0.351 to between 0.41 and 0.44. The early lesson came before Run 3. An earlier build used the filename as a fallback title. In that data, 42.8% of filenames carried the subclass name, and the insurance subclass F1 was a suspicious 1.0. I removed the fallback, republished the training set, and added a check to the build that fails if a filename-shaped title comes back. Subclass labels on the fast path are therefore not reliable, and I treat the fast path as a document-type decision only. Heads up. That sweep ran over the test-split windows themselves, and so did the decode sweep. The gate’s 0.97 confidence cutoff is a preset in the config (inherited from an earlier pipeline’s confidence bands), and the sweep landed on the same value. So the sweep describes the operating point; it is not an independent validation of the cutoff, and the 74.3% fast-path rate and the 0.013 error bound are optimistic. The final run (M9b) trained for four epochs with no class weights, a separate learning rate for the subclass heads and a logit-adjusted subclass loss; the repository’s training/run_m9a_local.sh --arm=m9b sets --weight-mode none --subclass-head-lr 1e-3 --subclass-logit-adjust 1.0 for these. uv sync --extra train uv run python training/train/train_modernbert.py \ --epochs 3 --select-on-subclass \ --label-smoothing 0.05 --subclass-label-smoothing 0.0 \ --input-construction v1 uv run python training/eval/eval_modernbert.py \ --checkpoint artifacts/pytorch/model --sample 0 --json --selective-risk uv run python training/eval/compare_runs.py --a <run_a.json> --b <run_b.json> Seeds and pins: every split and shuffle uses seed 42; the final run’s recorded settings were 4 epochs, batch 4 with 8 gradient-accumulation steps, learning rate 2e-5, subclass head learning rate 1e-3, label smoothing 0.05, and maximum length 8,192. The paired bootstrap uses 2,000 resamples at seed 42. Data sources are pinned to revisions in src/mailroom_ml/config.py. Cloud training needs a Hugging Face token and a Modal account and is gated on an explicit budget flag. Engineering quality 485 test functions in 33 test files, plus a shared conftest.py, covering calibration, windowing, routing, provenance, OOD, dataset build, evaluation CLI, training and deployment code. CI on pushes to main and on pull requests: ruff and pytest -m "not fullcorpus", with strict markers. Deploy-layer tests skip themselves when heavy extras are missing and never touch the network. Failure behaviour is explicit: if the model is missing, fails to load, or has a label mismatch, the document goes to the LLM path instead of getting a guess. Flagged out-of-distribution documents fail the fast path, and so do catch-all other predictions and subclasses with fewer than 5 training rows. A non-smoke Modal run exports ONNX and runs the parity check, and promotes the checkpoint only if both pass. Limitations and next steps The test split is small. With 323 documents, and single digits in many subclass cells, subclass F1 is noisy. The gate cutoff (0.97) is a config preset that the sweep over the test windows then agreed with, so it needs an independent check on fresh data. Contract and merger-agreement subclass heads are not fit for acting alone. Contract families such as services and supply are never recovered, and the merger head collapses onto a rare class. Insurance claims come largely from synthetic or rendered sources and are very regular. Real claims will be messier. The ONNX timings are from an earlier checkpoint on a laptop CPU. The final run was not re-exported. The next step is more training data for the contract families that fail, then one training run with a gentler prior correction. More epochs on the current recipe will not help, because validation contract F1 had already flattened. d: A ModernBERT document classifier with calibrated confidence, a routing gate that decides which documents can skip an LLM, and a leak audit that caught a label leak in my own training data.

b: Mailroom-ML ML training, evaluation & calibration At a glance 95.98% M9c document-type accuracy on 323 test documents (310 correct) 0.0189 M9c window calibration error (ECE), not document-level calibration 39.01% M9c confidence-only acceptance upper bound (126 of 323); not production fast-path coverage 4 of 4 M9c release gates met; this does not certify every subclass The current published release is M9c (m9c-20261014-113614), reviewed on 6 November 2026 against the source README at 01c2272⁠ and its held-out test report⁠. Conditional subclass accuracy is 229 of 310 scorable documents (73.87%). The 39.01% confidence-only figure omits support, catch-all, head-exclusion and subclass-projection guards; the full gate can accept fewer documents. Contract and correspondence remain excluded from fast-path routing by checkpoint policy. The M9b results below and the technical report preserve the earlier experiment history. They are not the current release’s metrics, and none of these evaluation runs was rerun for this site refresh. Published artifacts Trained model: mailroom-modernbert-classifier⁠. The M9c tag resolves to Hub revision 0910ad7, checked on 6 November 2026. The Hub card still describes the older M9a comparison, so use the tagged evaluation artifact and source report for the M9c numbers. Prepared training set: mailroom-modernbert-training⁠. A separate dataset with document-level train/validation/test splits and precomputed training/validation windows. It is not the classifier repository, and it is distinct from the public evaluation/ingress corpus, mailroom-dataset. M9c held-out measurement Result Scope Document-type accuracy 95.98% (310 / 323) Documents Conditional subclass accuracy 73.87% (229 / 310) Only documents with a correct type Calibration error (ECE) 0.0189 541 windows, not 323 document probabilities Confidence-only acceptance 39.01% (126 / 323) Upper bound before production guards OOD flag rate 5.57% (18 / 323) Diagnostic on this test pool The four specified #112 release gates pass. The separate report-only subclass target of 0.75 is not met (0.7387); passing the release gates is not a blanket subclass-quality claim. A reported M9c test-window sweep selects 0.94, but test-pool sweeps are diagnostics, not independently validated deployment thresholds. The problem A mailroom model reads incoming legal and insurance documents and decides what each one is. A large language model (LLM) can do that well, but it costs money on every document. Many documents are easy. A cheap classifier could handle those and pass only the hard or unfamiliar ones to the LLM. That plan only works if the classifier knows when it is unsure. A model that is 95% accurate overall but wrong with high confidence on some documents would quietly send errors downstream. So the project was less about raw accuracy than about three questions. Are its confidence scores honest? Can I pick a cutoff with a known error rate? Can I trust the training data to measure any of this? Approach I trained one ModernBERT encoder with a document-type head and one subclass head per type. Long documents are cut into overlapping 8,192-token windows, and the windows vote on the answer. Each head gets its own temperature scaling. A routing gate combines calibrated confidence, how much the windows agree, and the margin over the runner-up. A document takes the fast path only if the gate passes. Everything else goes to the LLM. The Mailroom-ML inference path: normalize, window, encode, classify with conditional heads, calibrate, flag out-of-distribution input, then route on a composite score either to the fast path or to the LLM sorter. What I built Training and evaluation pipelines in PyTorch with Transformers and Hugging Face datasets, run on Modal GPUs. Evaluation uses scipy and a paired bootstrap to compare runs. Calibration and routing. Per-head temperature scaling, a selective-risk sweep that finds the confidence cutoff for a 2% error budget, and an out-of-distribution flag from an energy probe on the logits. Data lineage. Every training set is pinned to a revision. A provenance module writes a byte-reproducible manifest with sha256 hashes and no timestamps, so a rebuild on the same inputs gives the same bytes. A leak audit. Early on, the model’s insurance subclass score looked too good. The audit showed that titles fell back to filenames, and 42.8% of filenames contained the subclass name. I removed the fallback and added a build-time check that fails if a filename-shaped title returns. ONNX export for CPU serving. An exported model is checked against the PyTorch one before promotion; the Modal serving app is a fallback. In the historical Apple M2 test with the earlier Run 3 checkpoint, fp32 matched PyTorch to within 4.25e-06 per head and int8 did not. That check is not evidence of M9c export parity. A test suite. The earlier audit counted 485 test functions in 33 files, not a current passing-test total. CI runs ruff and pytest; heavy-dependency tests can skip when torch or Modal is absent. Earlier results: M9b The numbers below come from the earlier M9b run. It trained for four epochs and was scored on a test split of 323 documents (541 windows). The test split was not used for training, for choosing the checkpoint epoch or for fitting calibration. It was used for more than one evaluation, though: I compared runs on it, ran a confidence sweep on it and ran the decode sweep described below on it. The 0.97 cutoff itself is a preset from the project’s config, and the sweep landed on the same value. Measure Result Document-type accuracy 0.9505 (307 of 323) Subclass accuracy, when the type is right 0.6287 Window calibration error (ECE) 0.0152, down from 0.0259 in the earlier run Documents passing the routing gate 74.3% Out-of-distribution flag rate 4.0% The M9b sweep looks for the lowest confidence cutoff whose accepted windows have an error bound under 2% and a band calibration error under 0.05. Lower cutoffs (0.87 to 0.96) met the error budget but failed the calibration check, so it comes out at 0.97, which accepts about 80% of windows (431 of 541). Scoring on the L4 GPU took 0.575 seconds per document. Heads up. The sweep that supports the 0.97 cutoff ran over these same test windows, and so did the decode sweep. That makes the fast-path and coverage numbers optimistic: they describe an operating point, not a validated setting. The tool that writes deployment thresholds refuses to run on a pool that contains test documents, so real thresholds are fit on the validation split. The M9b subclass heads were the weak part. Insurance claims reached F1 of 1.000, but that class is highly templated (114 test documents), so I would not read it as general skill. Merger-agreement F1 was 0.000 because the model put all 17 test merger agreements into one rare subclass. Contract subclass F1 was 0.162 against a 0.20 floor, leaving one acceptance gate failing. A decode-time adjustment did not fix it; the best setting reached 0.170. M9c later passed the release gates, but that does not make every subclass reliable. The figures are from an earlier 3-epoch run called Arm B, whose document-type accuracy is also 0.9505. “Arm A” and “Arm B” are the project’s names for two comparison runs: Arm A was a one-epoch smoke run and Arm B a three-epoch run with a heavier document-type loss weight. “M9b” is the four-epoch run in the historical table, not the later M9c release. These saved Arm B charts illustrate the earlier error analysis, not the current M9c checkpoint. Their original chart directories are not present in the current source tree, so the manifest records historical provenance rather than a currently reproducible upstream chart path. Which type each test-split document was routed to, from the earlier 3-epoch Arm B run. Subclass accuracy against how much each head collapses onto a single answer, from the earlier 3-epoch Arm B run. The full numbers, the calibration plots and the iteration history are in the technical report. What I learned A score that looks too good deserves an audit before it earns a headline. The insurance score was inflated by a filename leak, and fixing it made every number I report afterwards believable. Calibration changes what you can promise. Once confidence is honest, “send this to the LLM” becomes a measurable error budget instead of a guess. I rejected the smaller int8 export as the default. It saved time but changed predictions, and the parity check showed it. The fp32 export is what serves. Failing a gate is useful information. The decode sweep ruled out one fix cheaply and pointed at the real cause, which is data for specific contract types. Mailroom Reloaded uses this model as its first-stage bert_primary step.
