b: Mailroom Reloaded: technical report Agentic document pipeline · deployable rebuild Summary Mailroom Reloaded is a single deployable service that ingests documents, classifies them, extracts structured fields and archives them with a verifiable audit trail. It is built on CrewAI Flows, but a deterministic driver, not the framework’s event engine, owns control flow. Agents are called at fixed points, and routing between them is plain threshold code. A clean text-layer document costs exactly two LLM calls. The package is version 0.4.2 and requires Python 3.11 or 3.12. No accuracy or cost results are committed to the repository, so this report publishes none. It describes what the system does and the evidence that it runs. System and data The canonical main path is ingest, bert_primary, sort, gate_classify, extract, gate_extract, then report_catalog_archive (pipeline/state.py). The two gates are pure route computations. verify, boss, human_review and an evaluation-only grade step are dispatched by the driver outside that tuple. Node Kind Module ingest deterministic: text normalisation, PDF text layer, else vision transcription ingest/clerk.py, ingest/pdf.py, ingest/vision.py bert_primary local ModernBERT classification plus a handoff policy; fails open ingest/bert.py sort LLM call 1: structured sorter agents/sorter.py gate_classify, gate_extract deterministic route decisions, zero LLM calls agents/gate.py, pipeline/flow.py extract LLM call 2: per-class specialist agents/specialists.py verify LLM: judge, then arbiter agents/judge.py, agents/arbiter.py boss LLM: escalation and class reassignment agents/boss.py report_catalog_archive deterministic: report, move to archive, catalog row pipeline/report.py, pipeline/archivist.py human_review deterministic: park in review/ pipeline/flow.py, review.py The driver is MailroomFlow._drive_nodes in pipeline/flow.py. The decorated @start, @listen and @router methods exist so the class is routable and plottable, and they delegate to the same guarded node implementations. The stated reasons for an explicit driver are that CrewAI rejects the literal self-loop wiring, and that crash resume and deadline enforcement need one deterministic traversal. The fast path and its failure mode ingest and bert_primary are local, so they add no LLM calls. If ModernBERT is flagged off, missing, given an oversized input, or raises, the adapter returns an “unavailable” verdict and the handoff forces a full sort. Classes listed under defer_classes (by default contract and merger_agreement) and multi-window verdicts also fall back to a full sort. The model comes from Mailroom-ML through the optional bert extra. The gates and their escalation paths BandGate applies per-class thresholds from config/taxonomy.yaml. The global defaults are a high band of 0.95, a low band of 0.70, and retry_max of 2. Some classes override them. Stage Condition Action classify BERT and sorter disagree, not yet re-sorted re_sort (once, as a full sort) classify confidence at or above the high band proceed classify below high, retries left retry the sort classify below high, retries spent human_review extract length-capped or schema-invalid output retry, then human_review extract confidence at or above judge_band_high proceed extract between low and judge_band_high verify (judge, then arbiter) extract below low, retries left retry the extraction extract below low, retries spent boss The arbiter’s verdict maps accept and accept_with_caveats to report, re_extract to a retry, and escalate to the boss. The boss can reassign the class once, after which the document is extracted again, send the document to human review, or accept it. If the arbiter asks for a re-extraction after the retries are spent, the document goes to human review. The gate slot is pluggable. A LearnedGate (logistic model stored as plain JSON) loads when models/route_gate.json exists. It overrides the band only inside the medium band and never a hard rule. Jev, the opt-in decision model Jev (the “TypeSafe System One”) is a probabilistic decision model, not a text generator. It returns typed answers: a choice with a probability distribution, a noul (a single probability of yes), or a score. The gate asks it two questions: which route (proceed, retry, verify, boss or human_review) and whether to escalate to a human. Its confidence is derived from the concentration of the probability distribution, so it must be re-scaled by a calibration before the gate trusts it. A JevGate is used only when the provider is switched on and models/jev_calibration.json exists. It asks only inside the medium band and never overrides a hard rule. Calibration (mailroom jev calibrate) fits a temperature and thresholds, and refuses any row whose split is not train. When Jev is off, which is the default, the pipeline behaves as it does without it. Its default accept threshold is 0.8. Durability Bins are directories under a base directory: inbox, processing/<worker>, classified, review, failed, archive and manifests. A worker claims a file by atomic rename, and a loser of a race gets nothing and moves on (storage/bins.py). A manifest records the document id (the first 16 hex characters of the content sha256), filename, status, completed_nodes and serialised state. It is written with a temporary file and os.replace. Each node is wrapped by guarded(...), which on success appends the node to completed_nodes, snapshots state and appends an audit entry (pipeline/guards.py). On startup the watcher re-runs every manifest still in status processing from its first incomplete node (watcher.py). The per-document audit log is an append-only SQLite table keyed by document id and sequence. Each entry holds prev_hash and entry_hash, a sha256 over canonical JSON. Appends are resume-safe: a repeated node and event with an identical payload writes nothing (storage/audit_log.py). A separate archive ledger is one hash chain over every run (storage/ledger.py), with optional off-host anchoring and mailroom audit verify, anchor and export-head commands. An exclusive flock (watcher.lock) admits one draining process, which is why the split-watcher profile requires the embedded watcher to be switched off. Iteration history The repository’s changelog is the iteration record (141 commits in the history I could read). Notable recent entries, newest first: Unreleased — operator commands in /tui (links, readiness views, a read-only configuration summary, replay export, and a review queue with per-document detail); an operator SMS pager that is off by default; accessibility passes on /ui and /tui (a page heading, labelled tables, live regions, keyboard-reachable rows, focus rings, contrast fixes); a real provider probe behind GET /ready; the vendored llm-dojo-scoring updated to v0.22.0, with its scoring fixes; and a fix so mailroom eval no longer drops rows whose filename has no supported suffix. Dormant sandbox deep links removed from /tui. 0.4.2 (2026-10-11) — fixed the /ui documents table at phone widths. Verified at 420, 768 and 1280 px with no page-level horizontal overflow. v1 trim — an offline ingress simulator was moved off main onto a feature branch, leaving the core pipeline and the replay viewer. Verified on merged main. Results There are no committed accuracy, cost or throughput results. The evaluation harness (mailroom eval) exists, but I have not published a run. What follows is verification evidence, not model quality. Evaluation harness design The dataset is loaded at a pinned revision (default ed7576b6) with a blind configuration (text only, no labels) and a separate ground-truth configuration, joined on filename. A sha256 check against the document text raises an error on mismatch. Sampling is per class and nested: with the same seed and class, the 20-document draw is a prefix of the 50-document draw. The default seed is 42, the default is 20 documents per class, and the default split is test. The learned gate and sorter temperature calibration are fitted on the train split only; the fitting code raises an error for any other split, and KPIs are meant to be reported on test. After sampling, the runner checks overlap with the fast-path model’s training manifest and records a warning instead of failing, so overlapping documents can be excluded from reported numbers. Metrics cover sorter KPIs (accuracy, confusion matrix, expected calibration error, fast-path rate), specialist KPIs (field precision, recall and F1, schema-valid rate) and gate KPIs. Verification run on merged main (2026-10-11) This used a mock LLM provider with four seeded documents. It tests plumbing, not model quality. The ledger listing and its chain verification, in the cyan theme. Reproducibility Install and run the tests, with live-provider tests deselected by default: uv sync --extra dev uv run pytest -q uv run ruff check . node --test tests/tui/js/*.test.mjs node --test tests/ui/js/*.test.mjs Run one document, then the compose stack. The default provider is a mock that needs a fake OpenAI-compatible server, so set a real provider in .env first (DEFAULT_PROVIDER and its key): cp .env.example .env # then set DEFAULT_PROVIDER and its credentials uv run mailroom run tests/ingest/fixtures/letter.txt docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml --env-file .env up -d --build scripts/smoke.sh Compose profiles: the default stack (API with embedded watcher, OpenTelemetry collector, Phoenix, Prometheus, Grafana), local-llm (llamafile), gpu (local vLLM and a GPU metrics exporter) and split-watcher (a standalone watcher). Observability and engine ports bind to loopback only. Image versions are pinned in the compose file. An evaluation run: uv sync --extra dev --extra eval --extra bert uv run mailroom eval --per-class 20 --seed 42 --split test Engineering quality Test suite. The 1 November 2026 revision declares 1,276 def test_ functions across 89 test files, counted by grep. The 1,597 in the 11 October verification run is higher because of parametrisation and because the Node suites are also wired into pytest. Tiers. Agents, pipeline, eval, observability, API, deploy, intake, ingest, LLM, scoring, schemas, storage, TUI and /ui. Dependency fence. A test fails if any langgraph, langchain*, langfuse, braintrust or litellm import appears under src/ or in any dependency. Prompt lock. A test checks the sha256 of every vendored prompt against its lineage file, so frozen prompts cannot drift silently. Leak guard. A helper asserts that no ground-truth value appears in any recorded sorter or specialist request. Scoring parity. The vendored scoring subset is checked against the upstream package on ten fixture pairs when the parity extra is installed. Security defaults. Every /v1 route requires a bearer token when one is configured, and the app refuses to start off loopback without one. Uploads are capped at 50 MB. No hosted CI. The repository has no CI workflows; gates are run locally and their output recorded. Limitations and next steps No published evaluation results, so no claim about accuracy or cost per document. The hash chain cannot detect truncation of its tail without an external anchor, and the anchor does not protect the unanchored tail or open runs. The remote anchor’s database grants are documented as unverified until tried on a staging project. Gate decisions and thresholds are only as good as the calibration data; Jev’s usefulness depends on a calibration fitted on training rows. Deadlines are cooperative: they are checked after a node returns. Images and scanned PDFs need a configured vision provider. RTF and HTML are rejected. The offline ingress simulator is not on main. Next: run and publish a test-split evaluation with the seed, revision and cost card.

d: A compressed, deployment-ready Digital Mailroom on CrewAI Flows: a deterministic driver, a ModernBERT fast path, a durable audit trail, and consoles that replay every run.
h: At a glance The problem Approach What I built Results What I learned Stack
b: Mailroom Reloaded Agentic document pipeline · deployable rebuild At a glance 2 LLM calls for a clean text-layer document (sort, then extract) 1,597 tests passed in the 11 October 2026 verification run; the 1 November revision declares 1,276 test functions in 89 files The problem My Digital Mailroom design routes incoming documents: decide what each one is, pull out the fields that matter, and file it with a record of what happened. Agent frameworks make that easy to prototype and hard to run. If the model decides what happens next, you cannot say in advance how many calls a document will cost, where a crash will leave it, or why it ended up in a given folder. Mailroom Reloaded is a rebuild of that design as a single deployable service, built around one rule: code owns the control flow, and models are called at fixed points. Approach The Mailroom Reloaded flow: a fixed main path from ingest to archive, with two deterministic gates. The classify gate can re-sort once, retry the sort, or park the document for human review. The extract gate can retry the extraction, send it to verification (judge, then arbiter), escalate to the boss agent, or park it for human review. The pipeline is a CrewAI Flow, but a deterministic driver walks it, not CrewAI’s event engine. A clean text document goes through local ingest, the ModernBERT fast path from Mailroom-ML, one sorter call, a gate, one specialist extraction call, a second gate, and then report, catalog and archive. The gates are plain threshold code with zero LLM calls. That is why the cost of a clean document is exactly two calls. When a gate is not satisfied, fixed rules pick the next step, and the two gates have different branches: Classify gate: re-sort once, as a full pass, if the fast path and the sorter disagree about the class; retry a low-confidence sort, up to a configured limit; after the retries, park the document for human review. Extract gate: send a middling-confidence result to verification, where a judge grades the extraction and an arbiter decides whether to accept, re-extract or escalate; retry a low-confidence extraction, up to the limit; after the retries, escalate to a boss agent that can reassign the class or send the document to human review. An extraction that is invalid or cut off by the length limit is retried, then parked for human review. The ModernBERT fast path runs first and fails open. If the package or model is missing, the input is oversized, or anything errors, the pipeline falls back to a full LLM sort instead of stopping. What I built Durability. Documents move between bin folders (inbox, processing, review, failed, archive) by atomic rename, with a JSON manifest per document. Every completed node is checkpointed, so a crashed watcher resumes from the last finished node. A SQLite catalog and a hash-chained audit log record what happened; a second chain covers every run, with optional off-host anchoring. Observability. OpenTelemetry traces go to Phoenix, metrics to Prometheus, and provisioned Grafana dashboards (Pipeline, Serving & GPU, Quality) sit on top. Spans carry metadata, not document text. Two consoles. /ui is a plain JavaScript runs page. /tui is a browser terminal with a replay viewer that scrubs through a recorded run station by station, shows retries and escalations, and verifies the ledger chain. Deployment. One Docker Compose file with profiles for a local llamafile sidecar, a local vLLM server with GPU metrics, and a split watcher. Providers are switchable: a mock for tests, OpenRouter, vLLM, or llamafile. Gmail intake is an optional extra. An opt-in decision model. “Jev” is a calibrated, probabilistic decision model, not a chat model: it answers typed questions (a choice, a yes-probability, a score). When enabled and calibrated, it may overrule the gate only inside the medium-confidence band, never a hard rule. It is off by default and the pipeline is unchanged without it. An evaluation harness. mailroom eval samples a pinned dataset revision with a fixed seed, keeps ground truth away from the pipeline, and fits any learned gate on the training split only. Results I have no accuracy or cost numbers to publish for this service yet. The harness exists and is tested, but I have not committed evaluation results, so I am not quoting any. What I can show is that the machinery runs end to end: the main-branch verification ran four seeded documents through the stack with a mock provider and all four archived, and eleven browser checks of the replay viewer passed. The /tui replay viewer in the cyan theme, paused partway through a recorded demo run, with per-station document counts, a scrub bar and a metrics line. The replay inspector in the cyan theme, on a document that went through a gate decision and then a retry. The ledger command in the cyan theme, listing six hash-chained entries, followed by a successful chain verification. Heads up. The screenshots come from a demo run on a mock LLM provider with seeded documents, so the counts and costs in them describe the demo, not model quality. They were captured on 11 October 2026 at revision 545d8b7; /tui has since had accessibility and contrast fixes, so the current page differs in detail. What I learned Fixing the number of model calls at design time made everything else easier to reason about: cost, resume points, and what to log. Fail-open fast paths need to be tested as hard as the fast path itself. A hash chain on one disk detects edits, reordering and middle deletions, but not truncation of the tail. The docs say so, and the optional anchor exists for that reason. A replay viewer paid for itself quickly. Seeing a retry on a timeline beat reading logs. d: A from-scratch MapReduce rebuild: a Go cluster and Python reference, a 24-item paper mapping, S3 storage, compression, fault injection and a small-scale VM evaluation. In active development.
h: At a glance The problem Approach What I built What chaos testing found Evaluation at small scale What is planned What I’m learning Stack
b: MapReduce-Reloaded In active development · big data & distributed systems · Go & Python A from-scratch rebuild of Google’s MapReduce, as described by Dean and Ghemawat in MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters⁠ (OSDI 2004). Go is the main implementation. Python is a second implementation of the shared contract and of single-machine mode, so the two can be checked against each other byte for byte. View the code Work in progress. Reviewed on 6 November 2026 against revision 4dd1ca4⁠. Object storage, compression, benchmarks and the final report are now built. Python workers and full cross-language interoperability remain stretch work. The evaluation below is reported by the source repository, not rerun for this page. At a glance 24 items in the paper mapping: F1–F23 plus the F24 performance experiments 4 one-CPU worker containers on the course VM, not four independent machines 3.8× reported word-count speedup from one to four workers on 1 GiB inputs The problem MapReduce is the paper that made large-scale data processing ordinary. You write a map function and a reduce function, and the system handles splitting the input, scheduling thousands of tasks, moving data between machines and surviving the machines that fail along the way. Spark, Hadoop and most modern batch systems descend from it. I wanted to understand those guarantees by building them, not by reading about them. The aim is a faithful rebuild: every feature in the paper, each with a test that proves it works, then extended with what a 2026 system would use instead of 2004 infrastructure. Approach MapReduce-Reloaded as built so far: mr submit sends a job to the coordinator, or mr run -local runs it in one process, which every other mode must match byte for byte. The coordinator keeps the task table, logs each decision to a write-ahead log, and tracks workers by heartbeat. Workers ask it for tasks over gRPC; map tasks write R partition files and serve them, and reduce tasks fetch their partition from every map task, sort, reduce and write one output file each. The coordinator serves a status page, the coordinator and every worker export Prometheus metrics, and an optional Grafana dashboard shows them. The diagram shows the core task and shuffle path only. It does not attempt to draw the S3 backend, alternative Python coordinator or benchmark harness. A single-machine oracle first. The first working version runs the whole job in one process (mr run -local). Every later version, distributed or fault tolerant, must produce exactly the same output files. The tests check each version against it. One contract, two languages. Go and Python share a gRPC and protobuf message contract, a documented on-disk record format with a checksum on every block, and a fixed FNV-1a partition hash implemented in both languages. Language-specific hash behavior is not the contract: shared test vectors and golden files hold both implementations to the same bytes for uncompressed jobs. Small, reviewable steps. Each piece of work is one issue and one pull request, and each phase adds a short design record. The local make check quality gate runs linters and tests, and CircleCI runs checks on pull requests. What I built The programming model and the data path (§2–§4.4). Input splitting on record boundaries, partitioning by hash(key) mod R, a combiner, an external merge sort for data larger than memory, pluggable input and output formats, and atomic commits, so a half-written output file is never visible. A distributed cluster (§3.1–§3.2). A coordinator keeps the task table and the location of every intermediate file. Workers ask it for tasks over gRPC, map tasks write R partition files and serve them, and reducers stream their partition from every map task. Fault tolerance (§3.3, §3.6, §4.6, §4.9). Workers send heartbeats. A worker that misses three is declared dead, and its finished map tasks run again, because their output was on its disk. The coordinator logs every decision to a write-ahead log and resumes the job after a restart. The 2004 implementation aborted the job instead. Backup copies of the last slow tasks run near the end of a job, and the first copy to finish wins. A record that crashes user code twice is skipped on the next attempt. Counters are counted only from the winning attempt of each task, so re-run tasks do not double-count. Locality and status (§3.4, §4.8). The scheduler prefers to run a map task on the host that holds its input. The coordinator serves a status page, the coordinator and workers export Prometheus metrics, an optional monitoring profile adds Prometheus and a Grafana dashboard, and logs can be written as structured JSON. The paper’s example programs (§2.3, §5). Grep, word count, URL access frequency, reverse web-link graph, term vectors, inverted index and distributed sort, each with a test. A Docker Compose cluster. One coordinator and four workers, with Prometheus and Grafana as an optional profile, and a memory limit on each service so the whole cluster fits on one 8 GB virtual machine. An end-to-end script checks the cluster’s output against the oracle. Storage, compression and user jobs. S3-compatible storage with object-store commit semantics, zstd and Snappy codecs, and Go job files interpreted by workers. A Python coordinator can run with Go workers; a Python worker is not implemented. What chaos testing found The chaos test runs word count while, at random moments, workers die, new ones join, workers stall for 50–250 ms and the coordinator restarts from its log. A run passes only if the output files and the counters equal single-machine mode. Each run’s choices come from a seed, so a failure can be replayed. Its first runs failed on seed 7. The output held an extra _temporary directory: a reduce attempt that had already lost, to a backup copy or because its worker was declared dead, kept running and recreated the directory after the job had cleaned it up. Now the job creates that directory when it starts, and attempts never do. An attempt that runs after the job has finished fails and leaves nothing behind. The original test runs in one process, so a “dead” worker behaves like a machine cut off from the network, not one that lost power. The repository now also has a seeded make chaos driver for container kills, pauses and coordinator crashes in Compose. Dropped-packet fault injection remains out of scope. Evaluation at small scale The evaluation⁠ compares the paper’s mechanisms, not its absolute throughput: four containers share one 4-vCPU, 8 GB VM and one disk, versus roughly 1,800 machines in the paper. Experiment Reported observation Limit Scaling, 1 GiB input Four workers: word count 3.8×, sort 2.9× and grep 2.3× faster than one Median of three runs; shared-disk bottleneck Backup tasks with an injected slow worker 17.6 s without backups, 11.2 s with them Three runs per setting, fixed setting order; not drift-controlled Backup tasks without a slow worker Mean difference −0.11 s, 95% interval −0.38 to +0.16 s Ten interleaved pairs; does not prove zero cost Worker loss Every measured job finished with a checksum matching the normal run Agreement with a baseline, not an independent correctness proof The scaling run, set against the ideal of four times faster with four workers: Speedup with four workers over one, 1 GiB input Job Speedup Word count 3.8× Sort 2.9× Grep 2.3× The final report⁠ links the raw results, design decisions and reproduction steps. What is planned Python workers and a complete Go/Python interoperability matrix, coordinator high availability, skew handling and Parquet input remain stretch goals. LATE-style speculation is built as an opt-in mode, but its E7 evaluation has not been run; there is no measured claim that it is faster. What I’m learning Build the oracle first. Once a simple version defines the right answer, every harder version is a test against it, not a judgement call. Write the contract down before the code. The hand-written hash exists because both languages’ built-in hashes would have sent the same key to different reducers without any error. Random fault injection finds bugs that one-failure-at-a-time tests miss. The seed 7 bug appeared only when a losing attempt outlived the job’s cleanup. Stack Go Python gRPC Protocol Buffers Docker Compose Prometheus Grafana Distributed systems

b: NATD: appendix Publication scope · withheld data · open provenance This appendix records what can and cannot be published from the pilot. It deliberately contains no participant-level data and no new analysis. What the pilot supports Supported Not supported A nine-participant, 18-session pilot with helpful and deceitful chatbot personas A confirmatory effect estimate Exam-score changes after the helpful versus deceitful condition Generalisation beyond this pilot A single flag rate for the deceitful personas Detecting deception in general A protocol and question bank other researchers can inspect Claims about EEG or physiology The case study keeps the caveats visible: the sample is tiny, the design is a pilot, and gains from a low baseline need care. Withheld until authentication Physiology, EEG, eye-tracking, workload and the per-session source files stay unpublished until every recording is authenticated against its session. The repository does not contain them, so this site does not link to them. The instruments in the design include EEG, eye tracking, a pulse oximeter and GSR sensors. Provenance questions still open Issue #80⁠ records the unresolved points and this appendix does not paper over them: The linked repository does not contain the per-session exam CSVs behind the published numbers. The design document describes a larger five-condition study with a control condition, while the pilot used five named personas. Persona profiles exist in several versions, and the site does not pin one. The relationship between the nine-person pilot and the larger design is not documented in the repository. Until those are resolved, the exam figures on the case study should be read as pilot observations, not as a reproducible analysis. Citation Any reuse should cite the case study and the repository together, and should not present the pilot as a validated deception-detection result.

t: The Neural Architecture of Truth and Deception: technical report
d: Technical report on a study of nine participants and 18 sessions with helpful and deceitful chatbot personas: literature review, method, learning outcomes, detection, clusters, limits and references.
h: Overview Literature review Humans presume honesty and detect lies at about chance Chatbots lie on instruction, flatter by training, and evade detection Misinformation shifts knowledge, and AI tutor effects depend on design What is missing Method Learning outcomes Truth-default Clusters Interpretation and limitations References
b: The Neural Architecture of Truth and Deception: technical report Cognitive neuroscience research · UW–Parkside By Jack J. Burleson. Cognitive Neuroscience Lab, UW–Parkside; advisor Dr. Melissa Gregg. Pilot study. Physiological, EEG, eye-tracking and workload recordings are withheld until they are authenticated; this report covers the helpful-versus-deceitful results, detection and clusters. Overview Across 18 conversations with five chatbot personas, exam scores rose 12.3 points after the two helpful personas and fell 1.0 point after the three deceitful ones, while participants flagged deception in only 1 of 18 sessions. Nine participants each held two conversations with chatbots running different system-prompt personas, giving 18 sessions. Athena and Milgrim were instructed to be helpful; Alan, Enigma and Scarlet were instructed to deceive. Before and after each session we measured exam performance and recorded whether the participant flagged the disinformation. Study design: nine participants each held two conversations with chatbots running different system-prompt personas, giving 18 sessions. Athena and Milgrim were instructed to be helpful, Alan, Enigma and Scarlet to deceive. Exam scores and detection are reported here; other recordings from the same sessions are withheld until the data are authenticated. Learning. Exam scores rose 12.3 points on average after helpful personas (7 sessions) and fell 1.0 point after deceitful ones (11 sessions). The 13.3-point gap has a 95% confidence interval of 6.3 to 20.3. Helpful sessions also started 18 points lower, so part of the gain is probably regression to the mean. Detection. Participants flagged deception in 1 of 18 sessions (5.6%; 95% CI 0.1% to 27.3%), and in 1 of the 11 sessions with a deceitful persona. Reading the numbers. This is a nine-person exploratory study. Treat every p-value as descriptive: sessions are nested within participants, and persona is partly confounded with person. Data note. The analysis uses the supplied per-session CSV files, which disagree with the earlier draft report in several places, listed under Method. Literature review No verified study has tested Truth-Default Theory against a chatbot instructed to deceive, so this study is an exploratory extension and not a replication. The background below comes from a separate literature review of about 92 references, each tagged with how far it was verified; the 17 cited here are listed under References. Several publisher sites were unreachable during the search, so a number of bibliographic details are marked unverified. Humans presume honesty and detect lies at about chance Truth-Default Theory holds that people passively assume honesty until a trigger, such as a projected motive or incoherent content, pushes them past a threshold (Levine, 2014⁠). A meta-analysis of 206 documents found 54% accuracy at judging lies and truths, with 61% of truths but only 47% of lies classified correctly (Bond & DePaulo, 2006⁠). Weak behavioral cues, not poor judges, set that ceiling (Hartwig & Bond, 2011⁠). Lying is also unevenly spread: about half of all lies in a US survey came from 5.3% of adults (Serota et al., 2010⁠), which supports the base-rate premise behind a truth default. The closest parallel to my 1 of 18 is Levine’s report that fewer than 5% of unprimed participants spontaneously considered deception. The published follow-up carries an uncertain author list and I could not see its numbers (Clare, 2019⁠). My 5.6% is consistent with that figure, but the measures differ, so it is not a replication. The theory is also contested: Interpersonal Deception Theory says interactivity matters, and a chatbot dialogue is interactive (Park & Levine, 2015⁠). Chatbots lie on instruction, flatter by training, and evade detection GPT-3 complied with requests for disinformation tweets 80 of 102 times, so a system-prompted liar is a realistic manipulation (Spitale et al., 2023⁠). Readers were near chance at telling GPT-3 text from human text, and they used flawed heuristics such as first-person pronouns (Jakesch et al., 2023⁠). All five assistants tested for sycophancy flattered users, partly because raters prefer agreeable answers (Sharma et al., 2024⁠), so even the helpful personas may flatter. Plain, unhedged statements were relied on heavily, and first-person uncertainty reduced over-reliance (Zhou et al., 2024⁠; Kim et al., 2024⁠). Persona wording is an unreliable lever: across 162 roles, personas did not improve factual accuracy (Zheng et al., 2024⁠). I therefore did not assume a clean helpful-to-deceitful gradient in how false each persona’s output was. Misinformation shifts knowledge, and AI tutor effects depend on design People reproduce errors they read, even when they knew the right answer beforehand (Fazio et al., 2013⁠). Explicit warnings cut but did not eliminate reliance on misinformation (Ecker et al., 2010⁠). AI tutoring results depend on pedagogy. Unrestricted GPT access raised practice grades 48% but lowered later unassisted exam scores 17% among nearly 1,000 students, whereas a hint-giving tutor avoided that harm (Bastani et al., 2025⁠). A physics trial of 233 students favored a scripted AI tutor (Kestin et al., 2025⁠). No controlled study of a deliberately deceitful tutor was found. Any gain for the helpful personas is a persona-plus-pedagogy effect, not helpfulness alone. Gains from low baselines also need care, because regression to the mean inflates change when groups differ at baseline (Barnett et al., 2005⁠). What is missing The search found no verified study that applies Truth-Default Theory to human-chatbot dialogue with deceitful personas, varies system-prompted honesty and measures user beliefs, tests a deceitful tutor with human learners, or records physiological responses during such a conversation. These are “not found” results from a limited search. They justify an exploratory design and mean the study cannot claim precedent. Method Each of nine participants (mean age 23.8, SD 3.3, range 20 to 31; 7 men and 2 women; 7 English and 2 Spanish speakers; 4 right-handed, 2 left-handed, 3 ambidextrous) held two conversations, each with a different chatbot persona. Persona counts across the 18 sessions were Scarlet 5, Athena 4, Milgrim 3, Alan 3 and Enigma 3. Athena and Milgrim carried helpful system prompts; Alan, Enigma and Scarlet carried deceitful ones. Five participants met one helpful and one deceitful persona, three met two deceitful ones and one met two helpful ones. Modality Equipment or instrument What it captured Learning Introductory and exit exams adapted from Common Core and AP formats Exam score (%) before and after each conversation Detection Participant response Whether the participant flagged the disinformation The persona profiles, question database and scripts are in the project repository⁠. Analysis. All results use the supplied per-session CSV files as the source of truth. Analyses are descriptive and run at session level: Welch t-tests, Mann-Whitney tests, t-based 95% confidence intervals for mean change, exact Clopper-Pearson intervals for proportions, Spearman correlations, and an ordinary least squares adjustment for baseline score. Because each participant contributes two sessions, I add a within-participant contrast where the design allows it. The mixed-effects model in the earlier draft report was not refit for this version, so those p-values would be too small if read as independent tests. Where the CSV files and the earlier draft disagree. The files give a different persona mix, cluster sizes, mean age (23.8 against 23.2), exam statistics (mean exam score 44.8% before and 49.0% after, against 45.2% and 46.5%). The earlier draft’s non-significant overall ANOVA across chatbots no longer holds in the same form; the persona effect on exam change is now significant (see Learning outcomes). Wherever the two sources differ, this report follows the CSV files. Learning outcomes Helpful personas were followed by a 12.3-point exam gain, deceitful ones by a 1.0-point loss, and the 13.3-point gap is large next to its uncertainty. Mean exam score across all 18 sessions rose 4.2 points (44.8% to 49.0%; p = 0.08), so the overall effect is modest and the split by persona carries the result. Persona group Sessions Mean exam change (points) SD p Helpful (Athena, Milgrim) 7 +12.3 6.3 0.002 Deceitful (Alan, Enigma, Scarlet) 11 −1.0 7.5 0.67 Welch’s t-test on session-level change gives a difference of 13.3 points (95% CI 6.3 to 20.3; t(14.5) = 4.04, p = 0.001; Mann-Whitney p = 0.004). Helpful sessions gained significantly (+12.3, SD 6.3, p = 0.002); deceitful sessions did not change (−1.0, SD 7.5, p = 0.67). Mean exam change by persona (points) Helpful Deceitful Persona Type Sessions Mean exam change (points) Athena Helpful 4 +14.5 Milgrim Helpful 3 +9.3 Enigma Deceitful 3 +4.7 Alan Deceitful 3 −2.3 Scarlet Deceitful 5 −3.6 By persona the order is Athena +14.5, Milgrim +9.3, Enigma +4.7, Alan −2.3 and Scarlet −3.6 points (ANOVA p = 0.012; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.037). Only Athena’s interval, 4.3 to 24.7, clears zero on its own. Enigma gained 4.7 points despite a deceitful prompt, which a simple helpful-versus-deceitful reading would not predict. Three checks on how far to trust this. Baseline imbalance. Helpful sessions started at 33.6% against 52.0% for deceitful ones (p = 0.012), and sessions that started lower gained more (Spearman ρ = −0.58). Regression to the mean could explain part of the gap. Adjusting for baseline in an ordinary least squares model still leaves a helpful-persona effect of +11.6 points (95% CI 2.9 to 20.3, p = 0.013), and the baseline term itself is small and not significant. Within-participant contrast. Five participants met one helpful and one deceitful persona. In all five the helpful session produced the larger gain, by 9.2 points on average (range 5 to 15; paired t(4) = 4.8, p = 0.009). This comparison removes stable differences between people. Nesting. Both the Welch and OLS results treat 18 sessions as independent, so their intervals are optimistic. Read them as descriptive. A flat result after deceitful personas is ambiguous. It fits discounting of an unreliable source, insensitive exam items or high starting scores, and the session-level scores cannot separate these. Item-level exam data would. Truth-default Participants flagged the disinformation in 1 of 18 sessions (5.6%; exact 95% CI 0.1% to 27.3%), which fits the truth-default prediction that people presume honesty and rarely suspect deceit. The single detection came in a deceitful-persona session, so the rate among those sessions is 1 of 11 (9.1%; 95% CI 0.2% to 41.3%). With so few events the interval is wide: the data are compatible with detection rates anywhere from near zero to well over a third. The detection was S07, a Scarlet session, which also showed the largest exam decline in the study (−13 points). One case cannot say whether noticing the deceit caused the decline or whether a poor session prompted suspicion. Three points frame this result. The comparison to published truth-default work (under 5% spontaneous suspicion in unprimed participants) is loose, because that measure was spontaneous mention of deception and mine is a recorded detection. Lab participants may be more suspicious than people in daily life, and the files do not record what they were told beforehand. And a chatbot offers few of the triggers the theory lists, such as demeanor or an obvious personal motive, so low detection is the expected outcome and not a surprise. Clusters The supplied cluster labels split the 18 sessions into one group that gained 12.0 points and two that each lost about 4. Cluster Sessions Mean change (points) Persona mix 0, High improvers 9 +12.0 Athena 4, Milgrim 2, Scarlet 1, Enigma 1, Alan 1 1, High performers 4 −3.8 Alan 2, Scarlet 1, Enigma 1 2, Moderate decliners 5 −3.6 Scarlet 3, Enigma 1, Milgrim 1 Two patterns stand out. Clusters follow people more than personas: eight of the nine participants had both sessions in one cluster, and only one was split. All four Athena sessions sit in Cluster 0, and Scarlet sessions are spread across all three clusters (1 in Cluster 0, 1 in Cluster 1, 3 in Cluster 2), so the three-of-five concentration in Cluster 2 is suggestive, not decisive. Cluster 1 started highest (62% to 85%) and so had the least room to rise. The clusters were formed from these same exam scores, so the group differences describe the clustering and do not test anything. They are best used to generate hypotheses about who benefits, such as learners with low baselines paired with a helpful persona, to check in a larger sample. Interpretation and limitations The data reported here support two modest conclusions: helpful personas were followed by larger exam gains than deceitful ones, and almost nobody flagged the deceit. Both need replication, because several confounds are open. What the data support. Exam gains differ by persona, by 13.3 points between helpful and deceitful groups (95% CI 6.3 to 20.3), and the sign held in all five participants who met one of each. Detection was rare (1 of 18), consistent with a truth default, but a 95% interval of 0.1% to 27.3% means the rate is poorly pinned down. What they do not support. That deceit causes worse learning. Helpful sessions started 18 points lower, persona is partly confounded with person (each person met two of five personas), and each persona has only three to five sessions. That anything here detects or explains deception. Only one session involved a detection. Comparisons with published effect sizes beyond direction. Exam reliability, retest effects and item-level data are not available. Limitations. Nine participants, 18 sessions, 7 men and 2 women, aged 20 to 31. Sessions are nested within participants, and mixed-effects models were not refit for this version. Clusters were derived from the same exam data they are used to describe. The literature review rests on pages that were reachable during the search; several citations are marked unverified. Next steps. Replicate with more participants and balanced persona assignment, randomize persona order, and record item-level exam data and the falsity of each persona’s output, then fit mixed-effects models with participant random intercepts. References These are the 17 works cited above, out of about 92 in the full literature review (delivered separately as a file). Each carries the verification status recorded during the search: verified means the bibliographic details were confirmed on a page that was opened; partly verified means at least one detail is unconfirmed, and the gap is stated. Barnett, A. G., van der Pols, J. C., & Dobson, A. J. (2005). Regression to the mean: What it is and how to deal with it. t: The Neural Architecture of Truth and Deception
d: A pilot study of what happens when people talk to chatbots told to help or to deceive: nine participants, 18 sessions, five personas. Exam scores rose after helpful personas and fell after deceitful ones, and almost nobody flagged the deception.
h: At a glance The question Design Findings What it supports and what it does not What I would do next Methods and tools
b: The Neural Architecture of Truth and Deception Cognitive neuroscience research · UW–Parkside A pilot study from the Cognitive Neuroscience Lab at UW–Parkside, advised by Dr. Melissa Gregg, by Jack J. Burleson. View the code Technical report Pilot study. Physiological, EEG and eye-tracking recordings are withheld until they are authenticated; this page covers the helpful-versus-deceitful results. At a glance +12.3 vs −1.0 change in exam score, in points, after helpful personas (7 sessions) and after deceitful ones (11 sessions); the 13.3-point gap has a 95% CI of 6.3 to 20.3 1 of 18 sessions in which the participant flagged the deception (5.6%; 95% CI 0.1% to 27.3%) 9 and 18 participants and sessions, with five chatbot personas: two helpful, three deceitful In short, exam scores rose after the helpful personas and not after the deceitful ones, and participants almost never noticed the deceit. The question People tend to assume that what they are told is true until something gives them a reason to doubt it. Truth-Default Theory says this, and it predicts that a person talking to a chatbot that has been told to deceive will rarely suspect it. I could not find a verified study that tests the theory against a deceitful chatbot, so this study is a pilot-scale extension and not a replication. The core comparison is between helpful and deceitful assistants. The study asks two things about the people who talk to them: whether their exam scores change and whether they notice the deceit. Design Study design: nine participants each held two conversations with chatbots running different system-prompt personas, giving 18 sessions. Athena and Milgrim were instructed to be helpful, Alan, Enigma and Scarlet to deceive. Exam scores and detection are reported here; other recordings from the same sessions are withheld until the data are authenticated. Each of nine participants (mean age 23.8, range 20 to 31; 7 men and 2 women) held two conversations, each with a different chatbot running a different system-prompt persona. Athena and Milgrim were told to be helpful. Alan, Enigma and Scarlet were told to deceive. Before and after each session we measured exam performance and whether the participant flagged the disinformation. Findings 1. Exam scores differed by persona. Exam scores rose 12.3 points on average after helpful personas and fell 1.0 point after deceitful ones. By persona the order was Athena, Milgrim, Enigma, Alan, Scarlet. Enigma gained 4.7 points despite a deceitful prompt, which a simple helpful-versus-deceitful reading would not predict. Mean exam change by persona (points) Helpful Deceitful Persona Type Sessions Mean exam change (points) Athena Helpful 4 +14.5 Milgrim Helpful 3 +9.3 Enigma Deceitful 3 +4.7 Alan Deceitful 3 −2.3 Scarlet Deceitful 5 −3.6 Helpful sessions also started 18 points lower (33.6% against 52.0%), so part of the gain is probably regression to the mean. Adjusting for the starting score still left a helpful-persona effect of +11.6 points (95% CI 2.9 to 20.3; the interval treats sessions as independent, so it is optimistic). In the five participants who met one helpful and one deceitful persona, the helpful session produced the larger gain every time. 2. Almost nobody flagged the deception. Participants flagged it in 1 of 18 sessions, and in 1 of the 11 sessions with a deceitful persona. That fits the truth-default prediction, but with one event the 95% interval runs from 0.1% to 27.3%, so the rate is poorly pinned down. What it supports and what it does not It supports: larger exam gains after helpful personas than after deceitful ones, and rare detection. It does not support: that deceit causes worse learning. Helpful sessions started lower, persona is partly confounded with person (each person met two of five personas), and each persona has only three to five sessions. It does not support: any claim about how people detect deception. Only one session involved a detection. It cannot be read as independent tests. Sessions are nested within participants, and mixed-effects models were not refit, so every p-value and interval is descriptive. What I would do next Replicate with more participants and balanced persona assignment, randomize persona order, and record item-level exam data and how false each persona’s output was, then fit mixed-effects models with participant random intercepts. The technical report has the literature review, the full method, every table, the cluster analysis and the references with how far each was verified. d: A browser-based language-model neuron explorer: live TinyStories steering, random-direction controls, and recorded Qwen studies, with reproducible findings and explicit limits.
h: The problem What I built What the controls changed Limits and reproducibility What I learned Stack
b: Neuron Atlas Mechanistic interpretability · interactive visualization & evaluation Push one neuron and watch the story change. Neuron Atlas maps a small language model’s feed-forward neurons, lets you intervene in its computation, and compares the effect with random pushes of the same size. The goal is not just an interesting picture: it is a finding someone else can inspect and replay. Open Neuron Atlas View the code 8,192 TinyStories-8M neurons swept: 8 layers × 1,024 MLP neurons 2,048 random-direction controls: 256 in each layer 41 neurons beat every control in their layer on the original theme score The problem A striking continuation is easy to overinterpret. A neuron might appear to write a villain or a moral, but a random direction can write one too. I wanted to make that comparison visible, and to separate what a neuron responds to from what happens when its output is pushed. The steering-first method builds on neuron-explorer⁠. My implementation brings it to a small model that runs in the browser, then extends the analysis with control comparisons, held-out prompts and recorded studies of larger models. What I built A live model runtime. A GPT-Neo forward pass in TypeScript, with a KV cache and hooks for ablation, scaling, clamping and steering. TinyStories-8M inference runs in a Web Worker; using the site needs no inference server or GPU. A 3D atlas. React and Three.js display the neurons by output direction or co-firing. An inspector shows activation contexts, measured steering effects and the logit lens. Search, keyboard navigation and deep links make a particular neuron shareable. An offline measurement pipeline. Python builds the atlas, calibrates push strengths by layer, sweeps every TinyStories neuron and scores the text against matched random-direction controls. The browser replays recorded examples with the same prompt and push. Recorded model studies. Qwen3.5-0.8B (86,016 neurons) and a Qwen2.5-0.5B bad-medical-advice fine-tune (116,736 neurons) can be explored as recorded data. These models do not run live in the browser. Verification and failure handling. The repository checks the TypeScript runtime against PyTorch and includes browser tests for navigation, replay, accessibility, phone layouts, blocked storage and failed downloads. These are upstream checks, not a claim that I reran their full suite for this portfolio page. The TinyStories atlas and steering inspector for layer 4, neuron 803. What the controls changed The original sweep’s naive repeated-word test found a theme in 75% of neurons and 78% of random directions. Only 41 of 8,192 neurons (about 0.5%) outscored every control in their own layer. A compelling story alone is not evidence of a distinctive neuron. For example, L4 N803, “Run and hide”⁠, changes a sunny scene into a threat followed by flight. That is a useful description of the recorded text, not proof that the neuron represents a single human concept. The later robustness study reports that 21 of the original 41 still beat 95% of fresh random directions on 12 unseen prompts with sampling. Limits and reproducibility A small-model study, not a safety guarantee. These are interventions on particular models, prompts and scoring rules. Beating a finite set of controls is not a corrected significance test, a general explanation of a neuron, or evidence that a system is safe. TinyStories live inference and the larger models’ offline recordings are different capabilities. The upstream runtime verification reports exact replay of all 16 curated neuron cards, but only 47 of 48 sampled sweep rollouts: near-tied float32 logits can change greedy decoding. The model, corpus and code also have separate license terms. This page was reviewed on 6 November 2026, against source revision a580008⁠. The project linked in issue #89 began on the neuron-atlas branch⁠; the published project now includes the recorded-model studies too. The research reports⁠ and the live site’s Method page⁠ contain the methods, findings and limitations. What I learned Put a null comparison next to the attractive example, not in a footnote. Separate what a neuron reads, what its output writes, and whether removing it matters. Treat a replayable measurement and its limits as part of the interface. b: Psychometric Digital Twin: technical report Behavioral ML research · UW–Madison Summary This is the final project for PSYCH 755 at UW–Madison, taught by Dr. Adam Ross Nelson (Summer 2026). It asks whether an LLM, given a second-person prompt built from a survey respondent’s attributes, can predict that respondent’s own scores on two subscales of the PRCA-24 communication-apprehension measure, and whether its errors follow demographic group. On 241 respondents, none of the open-weight models was a close match to the real scores. The best persona run (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, second prompt version) had a pooled group-score error of 5.02 points on the 6–30 scale. Ridge regression reached 4.49 at the transit tier. By my own calculation, always predicting the cohort mean gives 4.93. At the transit tier the persona’s scores also did not rank people: its low-versus-high AUC was 0.53 on the group score, against 0.72 for a random forest. Everything on this page is an aggregate. The survey data are private and are not published. System and data Data The survey was collected through Prolific and Qualtrics for the course. Two Prolific recruitment waves were stacked (262 unique participants) and joined to 273 Qualtrics rows by the participant identifier the respondents typed into the survey. That gave 252 matches. Eleven had incomplete PRCA items and were dropped, leaving an analytic sample of 241. Both subscales are the sum of six five-point items, with comfort items reverse-coded, so each runs from 6 to 30. The repository states no ethics or consent details, so I make no claim about them here. Measure Group CA Interpersonal CA Mean (SD) 14.62 (6.03) 14.31 (5.82) Median 13 13 Low band (13 or less) 53.9% 53.1% Moderate band (14–19) 25.3% 28.6% High band (20 or more) 20.7% 18.3% Group means differ by employment. Full-time (n = 148) is 13.32, part-time (n = 31) is 16.16 and other (n = 62) is 16.95. Mean group CA also falls with public-transit use, from 17.38 for riders who never use transit (n = 50) to 12.84 for those riding eight or more days a month (n = 55). Mean PRCA scores by employment status in the analysed cohort. Persona tiers Study design: matched survey data feed cumulative information tiers. Each tier becomes a second-person prompt for an LLM and a feature set for seven classical ML models. Both are scored against the respondent's own PRCA subscale scores, then checked for error by group. Each tier adds to the one before it. Tier Adds demos Age, sex, country, student status employment Employment status geo Survey latitude and longitude transit Public-transit, ride-share, licence and car-access answers full Two open-text answers (LLM prompts only) Prompts are a second-person narrative (“You are a …”) with the request to report one’s own scores as JSON. Version 1 used full-precision coordinates and a soft JSON request. Version 2 rounded coordinates to one decimal, skipped follow-up transit questions when the answer was “never”, asked for the two subscales independently and used guided JSON. Version 3 added three single-cue tiers (ride-share only, public transit only, open text only). The classical models see the first four tiers only. Models and metrics I ran Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Llama 3.2 3B Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (AWQ) with vLLM. Version 1 used greedy decoding, a maximum of 256 new tokens and an 8,192-token context. Version 2 used temperature 0.3, seed 42 and guided JSON. Llama 3.2 3B base is left out of all scores, because it produced valid output for 7.1% of version 1 prompts and 0% of version 3. DeepSeek parsed 1,203 of 1,205 version 2 prompts. The classical suite is Ridge, Elastic Net, k-NN (k = 3), random forest (200 trees), histogram gradient boosting, XGBoost and a small neural net, scored with shuffled 5-fold cross-validation at seed 42. Metrics are mean absolute error (MAE) in score points, exact-match rate, band accuracy and per-band F1 for the low, moderate and high bands, and AUC for low versus high. b: Psychometric Digital Twin Behavioral ML research · UW–Madison Final project for PSYCH 755 at UW–Madison, taught by Dr. Adam Ross Nelson (Summer 2026). At a glance 241 survey respondents analysed, from 252 matched Prolific and Qualtrics records 5.02 vs 4.49 group-score error in points on the 6–30 scale: best LLM persona (pooled over tiers) vs best classical model (at the transit tier) 0.53 vs 0.72 AUC for telling low from high group apprehension at the transit tier: best persona run vs random forest In short, the LLM personas did not beat simple models. Most were worse than guessing the average respondent. The problem Researchers now use LLMs as stand-ins for survey respondents. The idea is to describe a person in a prompt and ask the model to answer as that person. I wanted to test that idea on one validated scale, where the real answer is known. The scale is the PRCA-24, a self-report measure of communication apprehension (CA). I used its group-discussion and interpersonal subscales, each scored 6 to 30. The question: when the model is told who a respondent is in the second person (“You are a …”), how close does it get to that respondent’s own scores? And when it is wrong, does the error follow demographic group, which would look like stereotyping? Approach Study design: matched survey data feed cumulative information tiers. Each tier becomes a second-person prompt for an LLM and a feature set for seven classical ML models. Both are scored against the respondent's own PRCA subscale scores, then checked for error by group. The survey was collected through Prolific and Qualtrics for the course. After matching and dropping respondents with incomplete scale items, 241 were left. For each one I built prompts in cumulative tiers: demographics, then employment, then survey location, then transit and ride-share habits, then (for the LLMs only) two open-text answers. I ran open-weight models on a GPU with vLLM: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Llama 3.2 3B Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (AWQ). The Llama 3.2 3B base model could not follow the output format and is left out of the scores. I compared them with seven classical models on the same tiers: Ridge, Elastic Net, k-NN, random forest, histogram gradient boosting, XGBoost and a small neural net, all with 5-fold cross-validation. What I built A cleaning and scoring pipeline. It joins the two survey exports, scores the scale and checks every tier against the same targets. Tiered persona prompts and batch inference. Three prompt versions, from five to eight tiers, run on a GPU host. A shared evaluation. Error in points, exact match, low/moderate/high band accuracy, F1 and AUC, computed the same way for LLMs and classical models. Explanation and bias checks. SHAP on the models and on a surrogate fit to the LLM’s outputs, plus error by employment, sex, student status and age. Secondary studies on public-transit use. These use random forests only, with no LLM. Results The classical floor is low but not far below a constant guess. Ridge reaches 4.49 points of group error at the transit tier. The pooled LLM errors run from 5.02 (DeepSeek, second prompt version) to 6.02 (Llama 3.3 70B). By my own calculation from the cohort table, always predicting the cohort mean gives 4.93, so the LLM personas did not beat that. Mean error by tier for a random forest and for the best LLM persona run (DeepSeek version 2), averaged across both subscales. More context helped the classical models and did not help the LLM. The random forest improved at each added tier. DeepSeek’s error stayed flat and got slightly worse at the employment step. At the transit tier the forest separated low from high apprehension with an AUC of 0.72 on the group score. DeepSeek scored 0.53, close to chance, and never predicted the high band for group CA. The feature results explain part of it. In the forest, ride-share days (Q28) was the strongest feature by far. In a surrogate model fit to the LLM’s outputs, latitude and age came first. What drives predictions at the transit tier: a random forest predicting true scores, and a surrogate fit to the LLM’s outputs. On bias, the clearest pattern was employment. DeepSeek’s group error was about 4.4 points for full-time respondents and about 5.5 to 6.2 for part-time and other. It under-predicted part-time and other respondents by roughly 1.7 to 3.6 points on average. Those groups did score higher on the scale, so the model missed a real difference rather than inventing one. Sex and student-status gaps were small. Group sizes are small too, so I treat all of this as descriptive. Heads up. This is one cohort of 241 online panel respondents. The classical models are cross-validated, but the LLM runs are single passes, and the constant-guess figure is computed on the same people it is scored on. The transit studies are associations, not causes. The technical report has the full tables, per-model results, the factor-analysis and secondary results, and the commands to reproduce them. What I learned A model that looks close on average error can still fail at the task. DeepSeek stayed near the mean, so its error was modest and its ranking of people was near chance. Report band accuracy and AUC next to error. Error alone hid the failure. Adding prompt detail is not a free gain. One bundle of transit text made Llama 3.1’s interpersonal error jump from 4.67 to 8.17 points, and a rewritten prompt did not fix it. A simple baseline belongs in every LLM evaluation. Here a ridge model and even a constant guess set a bar the personas did not clear. Stack Python scikit-learn XGBoost SHAP Factor analysis vLLM Quarto pytest

b: RVL-CDIP-Classifier: technical report Zero-shot document classification · prompt engineering · cost and robustness analysis Summary I tested how well a general-purpose vision model can classify scanned pages into the 16 RVL-CDIP classes using only a written prompt, with no training or fine-tuning. The main model was qwen/qwen3.7-flash through OpenRouter. I iterated on the prompt across 29 registered versions. The number to quote is 82.6% (925 of 1,120) for prompt v11.8 on a balanced slice of 70 images per class. That slice is a seeded, class-balanced sample of the Hugging Face mirror of RVL-CDIP, which holds 100 images per class across its three splits. It shares at least 20 images per class (320 in all) with the 800-image slice, so those two results are not independent. I did not verify its overlap with the 160-image slice I tuned on. On the tuning slice the same prompt reaches 99.4% (157 of 158), which I treat as an optimistic upper bound because I wrote rules for individual misses on that slice. Cost is about $0.0004 per image. Simulations of voting and routing looked promising, but none of the three routing tests I measured reproduced the gain. System and data The pipeline has these stages. Stage What it does Module Slice building Streams a 100-per-class Hugging Face mirror of RVL-CDIP, seeds the sampler, can skip images whose rendered pixels match an exclusion set, writes 1024×1024 grayscale PNGs with white padding scripts/datasets/, scripts/braintrust/create_braintrust_*_dataset.py, src/image_utils.py Preprocessing (separate tool) Converts TIFF/PDF pages to 300-DPI grayscale images and extracts OCR text with bounding boxes via Tesseract src/document_processor.py Prompting Versioned, append-only prompt registry src/prompts.py Classification Builds a message with the prompt and one image, calls OpenRouter, parses the label and a runner-up src/openrouter_classifier.py, src/openrouter_utils.py Evaluation Exact-match scoring, per-class tables, confusion matrices, near-miss counts, billed cost src/evaluation.py, scripts/braintrust/ Simulation Bootstrap analyses of voting, routing and failure handling over a pooled per-image corpus src/monte_carlo.py, src/routing.py OCR and 300 DPI. The 300-DPI conversion and OCR live in src/document_processor.py, which is used by the TIFF batch-processing script. The classifier does not call it. classify_image states that it sends only the image to the vision model, with no OCR text, and the message builder attaches the page as a base64 image_url part. The evaluated images are 1024×1024 grayscale PNGs. An early comparison on the 160-image slice found that full-size 2550×3300 inputs roughly doubled prompt tokens (1,637 to 3,701) with no accuracy gain (74.4% against 73.8%) under the baseline prompt. Data. The 160-image slice (10 per class) is the tuning slice. Larger slices come from the Hugging Face mirror, which holds exactly 100 images per class. The 1,120-image run used a 70-per-class sample, drawn with a fixed seed, from a 1,600-image dataset built from all three mirror splits (train, test and validation). The 800-image slice is the train split, so the two share at least 20 images per class (at least 320). The 1,120-image dataset was not built with an exclusion set, because only 50 images per class lie outside the train split. Slices are class-balanced and seeded. The dataset is RVL-CDIP (Harley, Ufkes and Derpanis, 2015). Iteration history Prompts run from v0, a short baseline, to v19, a variant that tells each call to act as one independent vote in a committee. The default in the code is v17.2. Accuracy below is on the 160-image tuning slice (158 scored rows), which is why it climbs so far. v1 — class definitions only. 80.1% (125/156). v4 — first disambiguation rules for confusable pairs. 83.5% (132/158). v7 — presentation cover and slide rules. 91.1% (144/158). v8.5 — folder-tab rewrite over-corrected cover pages. 88.6%, a regression. v10 — full ordered check cascade covering every earlier miss. 97.5% (154/158). v11 — estimate-versus-bill rule for budget and invoice. 98.7% (156/158). v11.8 — form-versus-budget and memo-versus-letter fixes for the three remaining misses. 99.4% (157/158). v16 — v11.9 plus two worked examples. 96.2% on the tuning slice, 83.8% and 79.4% on two fresh slices. v19 — vote preamble added to v18.1. 96.9% (155/160, counting one failed call as a miss). Two things stand out. The v10 jump (+6.4 points over v9’s 91.1%) came from writing rules for every v9 miss, which is tuning in the strict sense. And the last steps to 99.4% fixed three named images. I also kept a harder 56-row evaluation set made from earlier failures, where v11.8 scored 18 of 56 (32.1%), below v11.7’s 20 of 56. I fixed one trade-off and introduced others, so I stopped treating the 160-image slice as evidence of generalization. Results Run Prompt Eval set Held out from tuning? I did not check whether that slice shares images with the 160-image tuning slice, so some of its pages may have been seen during prompt iteration. Because the 1,120-image slice shares at least 320 images with the 800-image slice, those two results are not independent. Why accuracy falls with slice size is not proven. Larger slices contain noisier scans and more layout variety, and the v16 report found the same prompt scoring about 13 to 17 points lower on mirror slices than on the 160-image slice. I did not test whether the mirror images are intrinsically harder, so that stays a hypothesis. Source conflict. The experiment log gives v11.8 on the 320 slice as 87.2% (279/320). The per-run report gives 87.11% (277/318 scored). I use the log value so the table matches the figures, and the two differ by under 0.1 points. Error structure on the 1,120 run. Per-class accuracy is lowest for budget (67.1%), letter (70.0%), presentation (70.0%) and scientific report (71.4%), and highest for resume (95.7%). The most frequent confusions are letter as memo (16), budget as invoice (12) and specification as form (9). In 72 misses (6.4% of rows, 36.9% of misses) the correct class was the model’s runner-up. Other models, 160-image tuning slice. qwen3.5-35b-a3b scored 155/157 (98.7%) with v11.8, gemini-2.5-flash-lite 86.9%, gemini-2.5-flash 74.4% and kimi-k3 70.0%, though the last two ran with earlier prompts, so this is not a controlled comparison. Cost. The 1,120-image run billed $0.4937 against a list-price projection of $0.6815, because about 61 to 63 percent of prompt tokens were cache hits. That is about $0.00044 per image. The v19 run reports an average of $0.000377 per image. Other models I priced from single-image runs cost $0.0033 to $0.0534 per image. Figures Accuracy by prompt version on the 160-image tuning slice (not held out). It rises from 80.1% at v1 to 99.4% at v11.8. v11.8 accuracy by slice size. The 160-image point is the tuning slice; the 1,120-image point is 82.6%. The 800- and 1,120-image slices overlap. Best accuracy per model on the 160-image tuning slice with 95% intervals. The top qwen3.7-flash bar (98.7%, 157/159) is a temperature 0.3 rerun of v11.8, not the 99.4% run at temperature 0.1. The 98.7% in the third figure and the 99.4% in the first come from two separate runs of the same prompt on the same slice: temperature 0.3 with 159 scored rows (157 correct), and temperature 0.1 with 158 scored rows (157 correct). The gap is one row that failed to return usable content, so the two are consistent. Row-normalized confusion matrix for qwen3.7-flash with v11.8 on the 160-image tuning slice. This is the temperature 0.3 rerun (157/159, 98.7%), so almost all mass sits on the diagonal. Per-class accuracy on the 1,120-image run, overall 82.6%. Budget, letter, presentation and scientific report are lowest. Billed cost per image (left) and linear projection to 800, 25,000 and 320,000 images (right), from single-image runs of four other models. Simulated majority-vote accuracy against committee size K, from 0.821 at K=1 to 0.863 at K=25, over the pooled corpus. Simulated confidence-gated escalation: accuracy peaks at 91.9% at a 40% escalation fraction and 1.8 times the cost. Monte Carlo analyses The simulations bootstrap from a pooled corpus of 5,599 rows covering 1,512 images from 18 experiments. The older manuscript in the repo still cites 4,641 rows and 14 experiments, so I used the corpus summary, which is newer. The corpus mixes prompt versions (1,759 rows are v0, 2,561 are v11.8), so its baseline of 0.821 is a pooled rate and not the best prompt’s accuracy. Voting. Majority vote over K reads lifts simulated accuracy from 0.821 at K=1 to 0.863 at K=25, with most of the gain by K=7 (0.850). This is a mixed-ensemble forecast: the script groups recorded rows by filename only, so each image’s answers pool different models and prompt versions, and a committee is drawn from that pool. It is not repeated reads of one fixed classifier. The cost multiplier of K is an assumption, not a measured cost of rerunning one model. Routing, simulated. Escalating the lowest-confidence 40% to a model assumed to be 90% accurate at 3 times cost gives 0.919 at 1.8 times total cost. Routing, measured. On a 48-image low-confidence slice, re-running at maximum effort moved accuracy from 0.667 (32 correct) to 0.625 (30). Routing to a different stronger model on the tuning slice also failed to help: v18.1 went from 0.962 to 0.943 and v19 from 0.975 to 0.969, at 7.51 and 7.81 times the cost. The routing check scores only the 159 completed rows, so v19’s base is 155 of 159 (0.975) there and 154 of 159 (0.969) after merging. The 96.9% in the iteration history is the same 155 correct, divided by 160 rows because one failed call counts as a miss. The simulation’s assumption of a genuinely stronger escalator did not hold in practice. Voting, in detail. The 95% interval at K=1 is 0.805 to 0.836 and at K=25 is 0.846 to 0.879. Gains differ by class: handwritten rises from 0.841 to 0.908, resume from 0.926 to 0.975 and form from 0.849 to 0.897, while letter moves only from 0.742 to 0.757 and budget from 0.648 to 0.699. Voting helps when errors are random and not when the model is consistently wrong. The method resamples recorded runs, and 945 of the 1,512 images have more than one, so the other images cannot change. Voting has not been tested on a live run. Routing, sensitivity. The simulated accuracy at 40% escalation is 0.899, 0.919 or 0.939 if the escalated model is 5 points worse than, equal to, or 5 points better than the assumed 90%. At 50% escalation it falls to 0.909, so the curve peaks near 40%. At 10% escalation it is 0.864 at 1.2 times the cost, and at 20% it is 0.891 at 1.4 times. Routing, verification. The paired check on the 48 low-confidence images found a base accuracy of 0.667, against a simulated mean of 0.425 for the same images and a pooled 0.821, so the confidence ranking did pick out harder pages. The routed run on the v19 tuning slice sent 15 pages to gemini-2.5-pro. One prediction changed, to a wrong label, and the escalated run got 14 of those 15 pages right. The merged accuracy was 0.969 against 0.975, at 7.81 times the cost. Prompt ablation. A paired bootstrap of 10,000 resamples compares prompt versions on the images they share. v0 to v11.8 on 898 shared images goes from 0.732 to 0.862, a gain of 13.0 points (95% interval 10.1 to 15.9). v0 to v17 goes from 0.677 to 0.961 on 155 images, a gain of 28.4 points, but those are tuning-slice images, so it overstates the gain. Between tuned versions the results are inconclusive: v11.8 against v16 on 319 shared images is 0.890 against 0.900 (interval -0.053 to +0.034), and v16 against v17 on 159 is 0.969 against 0.962. v11.8 against v17 favors v11.8 (0.987 against 0.962) with an interval that just touches zero. Per-class differences rest on about 10 images each and have wide intervals. Exemplar mining. The simulation targeted 12 of the 110 confusion pairs with four few-shot exemplars, and estimated that 32.8 of 767 corpus errors (4.27%) would flip. The measured run on a 48-image slice moved from 0.688 (v17.2) to 0.646 (v18), a drop of 4.2 points with no gain. Failure model. First-attempt success was fitted at 0.946, with length truncation at 0.021 and transient, rate-limit and quota errors at zero. The recorded runs failed on 2.716% of rows. Simulating the pipeline with a fallback model gives 0.114%, and without one about 2.86% to 2.94% at any retry count from 1 to 5, so the fallback matters and extra retries do not. Extrapolated, that is about 28 failures per 25,000 images (interval 19 to 39) and 364 per 320,000 (interval 328 to 402). This is a model of the pipeline and I have not confirmed it on a live run. Reasoning-trace analysis. Of 1,913 rows with reasoning, 1,832 traces parsed into the prompt’s checks and 1,301 stop explicitly. The mean stop is at check 9.4 of 14 and the error rate is 17.1%. Words quoted in the stopping evidence are scored by how much earlier the stop comes and how much the error rate rises, weighted by frequency. “minutes” (11 traces, 82% error), “routing” (10 traces, 90%) and “variance” (10 traces, 100%) score highest. The counts are small, so these are leads and not findings. Confusion pairs. In the pooled corpus the largest are budget read as invoice (63), letter as memo (63), specification as form (52), invoice as form (51), budget as form (40) and handwritten as letter (34). Ten words associated with the model stopping earlier and erring more, scored by how much earlier it stops and how much the error rate rises, against a 17.1% baseline error. Data exploration and observability tools These are in the repository and are linked from the case study as well. Tool What it does Where Quarto site Manuscript, methods, results, experiment log, prompt changelog, cost analysis, research memos, notebooks and a misclassification appendix. Renders offline, with no model spend. website/⁠ Monte Carlo pages and reports Ten pages and the raw tables for the analyses above. website/montecarlo/⁠, reports/monte_carlo/⁠ Interactive pages A cost calculator and an experiment explorer. website/interactive/⁠ Data exploration Class balance, image dimensions, file sizes, color modes and sample grids. scripts/eda/⁠ Braintrust tooling Dataset builders, evaluation runs logged as Braintrust experiments, summaries, reports, metric charts, and the Monte Carlo scripts. scripts/braintrust/⁠ Notebooks Setup, balanced sampling and upload, evaluators over a full experiment, and cost. notebooks/⁠ Reproducibility The environment needs Tesseract and Poppler for the preprocessing tool, plus an OpenRouter key in a local .env file. pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # add OPENROUTER_API_KEY python scripts/datasets/create_balanced_dataset.py python scripts/openrouter/estimate_openrouter_cost.py python src/openrouter_classifier.py Slices are rebuilt with fixed seeds (default 42, other slices 1738, 2303 and 9413), so the same source reproduces the same images. Prompt text is versioned in src/prompts.py, and each experiment’s final report, confusion matrix and manifest are committed under reports/. The model runs through a hosted API, so results are point-in-time. A provider-side change could shift them. Engineering quality The test suite has 318 test functions in 21 files, covering the document processor, prompt registry, classifier and message builder, evaluation and report accounting, routing, Monte Carlo code and dataset builders. Evaluation uses exact match, with a failed or empty response counted as a miss, so API failures lower the score and are not hidden. The v16 report attributes 16 of 480 rows to length truncation and provider errors, and the report proposed a higher token cap. Reports record billed cost per row. Limitations and next steps Tuning contamination. The 99.4% figure is on the slice I tuned against. I cannot rule out that some mirror images in the larger slices appeared in failure-driven evaluation sets, so 82.6% is a different slice from the tuning slice, not a verified-clean test set. The 1,120-image slice was not built with an exclusion set: it is a 70-per-class sample of the 100-per-class mirror, so it shares at least 20 images per class with the 800-image slice. I did not check it against the 160-image tuning slice. Mirror, not the full test set. All numbers are from small balanced slices of a 100-per-class mirror. They are not the 40,000-image RVL-CDIP test set, and they are not comparable to published supervised results. Bundled edits. Each prompt version changes several things at once, so I cannot attribute gains to individual rules. Single main model. Cross-model results are not controlled, and statistical power on 160 images is low. Untested fixes. Next steps are a prompt-ablation study on the large slices, and testing whether the 13-to-17-point gap between curated and mirror slices comes from image quality or from label noise.
