b: RVL-CDIP-Classifier Vision LLMs & prompt engineering At a glance 82.6% accuracy on 1,120 images (925 correct). The slice shares at least 320 images with the 800-image slice; overlap with tuning not verified 99.4% on the 160-image slice I tuned against, so an optimistic number 29 registered prompt versions, v0 to v19 ≈ $0.0004 per image for the main model The 29-version registry includes subversions such as v11.8 and v17.2; “v0 to v19” names the endpoints, not 20 consecutive integer-only entries. The problem RVL-CDIP is the standard benchmark for document-type classification: scanned pages from a tobacco-litigation archive, sorted into 16 classes such as invoice, memo, letter and budget. Models trained for it usually need labeled data and a fine-tuning pipeline. I wanted to know how far a general-purpose vision model could get with no training at all, using only the prompt, and what that would cost. Approach The model gets the page image and a long written prompt. The prompt names the 16 classes and then walks through an ordered list of checks, so that a page is judged by what it does rather than what it is about. I changed the prompt one version at a time and scored every version the same way, so each change could be traced to a number. The RVL-CDIP prompt study pipeline: a balanced, seeded slice of page images is preprocessed and sent with a versioned prompt to a vision LLM; answers are parsed, scored by exact match, logged, and analysed with Monte Carlo simulation. What I built Preprocessing tools. A document processor converts TIFF and PDF pages to 300-DPI grayscale images and runs Tesseract OCR to get text with bounding boxes. The classifier path. The evaluated classifier does not use that OCR output. It sends the vision model only a 1024×1024 grayscale image plus the prompt, through OpenRouter. Versioned prompts. src/prompts.py holds every version, append-only, with a registry I can query by name. Evaluation harness. Balanced, deduplicated slices of the dataset, exact-match scoring, per-class tables, confusion matrices, billed-cost tracking, and a Monte Carlo module that simulates voting and routing on top of the measured results. Tests. 318 test functions across 21 test files. Results On the 160-image slice, accuracy climbed from 80.1% at v1 to 99.4% at v11.8. That is a tuning-slice number. I read the misses on that slice and wrote rules for them, so it overstates what the prompt can do on pages it has not seen. Accuracy of qwen3.7-flash on the 160-image tuning slice across prompt versions, rising from 80.1% at v1 to 99.4% at v11.8. The honest headline comes from larger slices. The same v11.8 prompt scored 82.6% on a balanced 1,120-image slice. That slice is a seeded, class-balanced sample of 70 images per class from the Hugging Face mirror of RVL-CDIP, which holds 100 per class across its three splits. The 800-image slice is the mirror’s train split (50 per class), so the two slices share at least 20 images per class, 320 in all, and the 83.1% and 82.6% results are not independent. I did not verify whether the 1,120-image slice shares images with the 160-image tuning slice. Across slice sizes it scored 87.2% at 320 images, 89.1% at 476 scored images, and 83.1% at 800. On that 800-image slice, the untuned v0 prompt scored 66.1%, so the prompt work is worth about 17 points on that slice. I did not check whether the 800-image slice shares images with the 160-image tuning slice either. v11.8 accuracy by slice size: 99.4% on the 160-image tuning slice, then 87.2%, 89.1%, 83.1% and 82.6% on larger slices. The 800- and 1,120-image slices overlap. Heads up. The 160-image points in both charts come from the slice I iterated on. The 1,120-image point is the one to quote. The 1,120-image slice shares at least 20 images per class with the 800-image slice, so those two results are not independent evidence. I did not check it against the 160-image tuning slice or the other earlier slices, so it may share images with them. Treat it as a better estimate than the tuning slice, not as a clean test. Where it fails is consistent. Budget (67.1%), letter (70.0%), presentation (70.0%) and scientific report (71.4%) are the weak classes on the 1,120 run, and the most common single error is letter predicted as memo (16 cases). In 72 of the misses, the correct class was the model’s own runner-up. What the simulations showed The repository’s Monte Carlo scripts treat every recorded run as a draw from a per-image distribution of answers, then resample it to ask “what if” questions without spending any model credits. They work on a pooled corpus of 5,599 rows covering 1,512 images from 18 experiments. The corpus mixes prompt versions and models, so its 82.1% baseline is a pooled rate and not the best prompt’s accuracy. For the same reason, a “read” in the voting forecast is a draw from that mixed pool, not a repeat of one fixed classifier. Question What the simulation said What I measured Would majority voting help? Forecast from the pooled, mixed-model corpus, not repeated reads of one fixed classifier: 7 reads, 85.0%; 25 reads, 86.3%. Cost is assumed to scale with the number of reads; it is not a measured rerun cost. Not tested on a live run. Would sending the least-confident pages to a stronger model help? The least-confident 40%: 91.9% at 1.8 times the cost, if the stronger model is 90% accurate at 3 times the cost. Down, not up. On a 48-image low-confidence slice, 66.7% became 62.5%. On the tuning slice, v19 went from 97.5% to 96.9% at 7.8 times the cost. Would a few worked examples for the commonest confusions help? About 4.3% of errors fixed (33 of 767). Down. On a 48-image slice, 68.8% became 64.6%. Which prompt changes were real? A paired bootstrap on shared images puts v0 to v11.8 at +13.0 points (95% interval 10.1 to 15.9, 898 images). This one is a test of measured runs, not a forecast. Would retries and a fallback model cover API failures? With a fallback, 0.11% of calls fail, against about 2.9% without one. Extra retries barely matter. Modelled only. Both changes the simulation favoured lowered measured accuracy, and escalation did so on the tuning slice too: Measured exact-match accuracy before and after each change Before After Change Before After Escalation, 48-image low-confidence slice 66.7% 62.5% Worked examples, 48-image slice 68.8% 64.6% Escalation of v19, tuning slice 97.5% 96.9% Four findings stood out. Voting fixes noisy errors, not consistent ones. The simulated gain concentrates in classes like handwritten (84.1% to 90.8% at 25 reads). Letter barely moves (74.2% to 75.7%) and budget stays near 70%. When the model is wrong about a page every time, asking again does not help. The method also resamples recorded runs, and only 945 of the 1,512 images have more than one, so the rest cannot change. The confidence ranking found hard pages, but the stronger model did not fix them. The 48 lowest-confidence pages scored 66.7% on the base run, against 82.1% pooled, so the ranking was informative. When I routed the tail to a stronger model on the tuning slice, 15 pages went through, one answer changed, and it changed to a wrong label. A sensitivity sweep says the plan needs the escalated model to be better on exactly those pages (89.9% to 93.9% at 40% escalation for a 5-point swing either way), and neither escalation I tried was. Most of the prompt gain came early. The jump from the baseline prompt to a rule-based one is real. The later versions are statistically indistinguishable from each other: v11.8 against v16 on 319 shared images is 89.0% against 90.0%, with an interval from about -5 to +3 points. The +28.4-point gain for v17 over v0 is measured on 155 images from the tuning slice, so I quote the 898-image figure instead. Errors cluster in a few pairs. Budget read as invoice (63 cases), letter as memo (63), specification as form (52) and invoice as form (51) are the largest confusion pairs in the pooled corpus. I also mined the reasoning traces for the words that appear when the model stops checking early. The prompt works through up to 14 checks in order, and the typical trace stops at check 9.4. Words such as “minutes”, “routing” and “variance” show up in traces that stop early and are wrong far more often than the 17.1% baseline error rate. Each appears in only 10 or 11 traces, so these are leads to test and not findings. Ten words associated with the model stopping earlier and erring more, scored by how much earlier it stops and how much the error rate rises, against a 17.1% baseline error. Simulated confidence-gated escalation: accuracy peaks at 91.9% at a 40% escalation fraction and 1.8 times the cost. Heads up. These are resampled results from recorded runs, not new experiments. Two of the forecasts I tested by measurement, routing and worked examples, and neither held up. Voting and the failure model are untested, and the word list rests on small counts. The report has the full tables. Explore the data and tools The repository ships the tooling I used to look at the data and to watch the runs, and a Quarto site that pulls the results together. The site renders offline with no model spend. The Quarto documentation site⁠ has the manuscript, methods, results and experiment logs, the prompt changelog, cost analysis, short research memos, notebooks and a misclassification appendix. Monte Carlo pages⁠ are ten pages covering the analyses behind this section, and the raw reports⁠ hold the tables, including voting, routing, prompt ablation, the failure model, exemplar mining and the word analysis. Interactive pages⁠ include a cost calculator and an experiment explorer. Data exploration scripts⁠ profile the dataset: class balance, image dimensions, file sizes, color modes and sample grids. Braintrust tooling⁠ builds the datasets, runs evaluations that are logged as Braintrust experiments, and writes summaries, reports and metric charts. The Monte Carlo scripts live there too. Notebooks⁠ walk through setup, balanced sampling and upload, evaluators over a full experiment, and cost. What I learned Tuning accuracy is not accuracy. Fixing named misses one by one pushed the tuning slice to 99.4% while larger slices stayed in the low 80s. Later versions made this worse in places: a longer v16 prompt dropped to 96.2% on the tuning slice and scored 83.8% and 79.4% on two fresh slices. Simulation needs a measurement behind it. The Monte Carlo model suggested sending the least-confident pages to a stronger model. When I ran that, accuracy went down slightly (96.2% to 94.3% on the tuning slice) at about 7.5 times the cost. More resolution did not help. Full-size 2550×3300 images doubled prompt tokens and did not improve accuracy in an early comparison. b: Wave Laboratory: technical report Side project · simulation & graphics Launch the lab Summary Wave Laboratory is a browser-based ocean-wave and ship-motion sandbox: it builds a sea state from oceanographic spectra, synthesises the surface with FFTs, floats 6-degree-of-freedom ships in it and records the results with virtual instruments. It is a personal project under the MIT license, version 0.1.0. It needs Node 22 or later to build and a browser with WebGL 2 to run. The conventions in docs/PHYSICS.md are the single source of truth for both the CPU physics and the GPU renderer; the document states that if code and file disagree, that is a bug. This is a simulation tool. It has been checked against analytic and textbook results, listed below, and not against measurements from a wave tank or sea trial. System and data Physics models Linear waves. Dispersion is ω² = (g k + (σ/ρ) k³) tanh(k h), with finite depth h and surface tension σ. Dynamic pressure attenuates with depth by cosh(k(z+h)) / cosh(kh). Below the surface, pressure uses Wheeler stretching. Spectra. Each wave system has an energy spectrum, a directional spreading function and a seed. The table gives what is implemented. Model Role Key parameters and notes JONSWAP Developing wind sea α, peak frequency ω_p, peak enhancement γ (3.3 used for focused groups), σ = 0.07 below and 0.09 above the peak; normalised so 4√m₀ = H_s Pierson–Moskowitz Fully developed sea JONSWAP with γ = 1, normalised to H_s Bretschneider Two-parameter sea Same family as above, normalised to H_s TMA Finite-depth correction Kitaigorodskii depth factor, applied when depth is under 1000 m; H_s re-normalised Hasselmann et al. (1973) Fetch-limited wind sea Growth with fetch, capped at the fully developed limit, H_s ≈ 0.209 U²/g Regular (Airy) Single analytic wave η = a cos θ; a second-order Stokes harmonic is added when choppiness is above zero NewWave (Tromans et al. 1991) Focused rogue group 40 linear components between 0.6 ω_p and 3 ω_p, phased so crests coincide at a chosen place and time Directional spreading is one of cos-2s, Mitsuyasu (frequency dependent) or Donelan–Banner sech², each normalised so the integral over direction is 1. A uniform surface current Doppler-shifts the whole sea. Surface synthesis. The surface is a sum of four periodic cascades with sizes 1024, 256, 64 and 16 m. The first three are evaluated by the CPU physics on 128 by 128 grids; the fourth runs to the grid limit and is visual only. Initial amplitudes h₀(k) are made once on the CPU from a counter-based hash of the system seed, cascade and wavenumber index, so every grid resolution sees the same sea. Horizontal choppy displacement uses a choppiness factor, and the Jacobian of the displacement flags folding: J below zero marks a breaking crest, which drives foam. Rogue waves. A focused wave adds to the background sea, so the crest at the focus sits above it by the chosen crest amplitude. The inspector compares the equivalent steepness with the Miche limit, 0.142 tanh(kh). The note records Draupner as 18.5 m over 11.9 m, a crest-to-H_s ratio of 1.55, in a typical recorded range of 1.2 to 1.6. Ships. Hull forces come from integrating pressure over the instantaneous wetted hull, as hydrostatics plus Froude–Krylov, sampled on up to 280 water columns. Added mass uses strip theory with Lewis-form sections and a three-dimensional end reduction. Radiation damping is tuned to 15 per cent of critical in heave and pitch, and roll damping follows an Ikeda-type decomposition. Wind acts through frontal and lateral areas with drag coefficients of 0.7 and 0.9. Square sails, flooding through watertight compartments with free-surface loss of stability, and an elastic catenary anchor line are modelled; each has its own section in the physics note. Weather. Gusts come from 24 Fourier modes drawn from a von Kármán spectrum, carried downwind as frozen turbulence. Whitecap coverage follows Monahan and O’Muircheartaigh (1980), visibility follows Koschmieder’s law with a rain term, and lightning is visual only. Instruments. Welch’s method gives spectra from Hann-windowed segments with 50 per cent overlap, scaled so the integrated density equals the signal variance. Zero-up-crossing statistics follow IAHR and PIANC conventions. Motion-sickness incidence follows O’Hanlon and McCauley (1974). Underwater optics. Jerlov water types give diffuse attenuation coefficients K_d for red, green and blue. They drive rendering only, not the physics. Light is attenuated as c·e^(−K_d·d) plus in-scattered colour, and from below the surface shows the rippled sky inside Snell’s window (48.6°) and a mirror outside it. Architecture The main thread runs the React UI, a Zustand store and the renderer. A Web Worker runs the simulation: the CPU ocean field, the vessels and a fixed-rate recorder. SimClient keeps one request in flight. Edits go through a Zod-validated store, which also keeps undo history and bumps a revision that reloads the worker. Stage Module path Maths, RNG, fixed-step clock, units src/core/ Experiment schema (Zod) and presets src/schema/ Dispersion, spectra, spreading, cascades, CPU FFT src/ocean/ Hulls, hydrostatics, hydrodynamics, wind, sails, flooding, mooring src/vessel/ Gusts, squalls, rain, lightning src/weather/ Welch PSD, statistics, MSI src/instruments/ Simulation kernel, worker, client src/sim/ WebGL 2 renderer, GPU FFT ocean, post stack, underwater pass src/render/ React application src/ui/ Only src/render imports Three.js. The renderer is the sole GPU dependency and is isolated behind render/api.ts. Performance budget at default settings: one CPU ocean snapshot (three cascades, six 128 by 128 FFTs each) takes about 15 ms in the worker at 20 Hz, and a vessel step takes under 1 ms per vessel at 120 Hz. The GPU FFT (four cascades at 256 by 256) takes a few milliseconds. The GPU and CPU cross-check The GPU inverse-FFTs the same h₀ amplitudes the CPU uses. On each new sea the renderer reads one texel back, compares it with the CPU transform and calls console.error on a mismatch, which e2e/app.spec.ts fails on. Devices without 32-bit float render targets use half-float and skip the readback. The GPU draws only elevation and horizontal displacement; slope, Jacobian and foam are finite differences of the displaced surface, and pressure and orbital velocity stay on the CPU. Iteration history The current snapshot (revision 4c7354e, 24 October 2026) has 174 commits. The earlier report recorded 131 commits from 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-08; this page now uses the later count. The plan document’s status table lists what shipped in v0.1. Core — tooling, schema, deterministic fixed-step core. Shipped. Ocean — spectra, wind-sea growth, spreading, four cascades, choppy displacement, regular waves, CPU reference and GPU. Shipped. Vessels — pressure integration with waterline clipping, radiation, viscous drag, propulsion, rudder and autopilot. Shipped. Damage, moorings, instruments, UI — flooding, anchors, Welch PSD, MSI, CSV export, presets, share links, phone layout. Shipped. Rendering extras — HDR post stack with bloom, underwater camera with Snell’s window. Shipped. Results There are no benchmark numbers against external data. The evidence is the validation suite below. Validation suite The longer statistical checks live in *.validation.ts files and run with pnpm validate, with a 120-second timeout per test. There are 9 files and 25 test definitions. File What it checks ocean/ocean.validation.ts A virtual wave gauge reproduces the requested JONSWAP spectrum; linear seas have Gaussian elevations and H1/3 close to Hm0; choppy seas show positive skewness (sharper crests) sim/rogue.validation.ts A 12 m NewWave crest peaks at the focus gauge near t = 75 s and the ship ships green water vessel/vessel.waves.validation.ts Heave RAO close to 1 for 20 s head seas; slamming and green water in steep head seas vessel/vessel.manoeuvring.validation.ts Plausible steady speeds, 30° autopilot turns without large overshoot, rudder sign and rate limit vessel/vessel.wind.validation.ts Leeway and heel in a beam wind, carrier course holding, square-rig sailing, reefing in a storm vessel/flooding.validation.ts, damage.validation.ts Flooding and damage behaviour, including Torricelli decay and flooded-barge roll period vessel/mooring.validation.ts A trawler in a 15 m/s wind settles at a chain pull of 3.9 kN against a 3.8 kN wind load; a cargo ship stays within its watch circle in a 2 m swell; the anchor drags in a 45 m/s gale vessel/vessel.perf.validation.ts Performance check The physics note also records that the simulated roll period of a flooded barge matches the closed-form value within 1 per cent, and that the elastic catenary was compared with a direct numerical integration of the governing equations for three stiffnesses. Test counts These are counts of test definitions found by grep, not a run result. I did not run the suite for this report, so I make no pass-rate claim. Suite Count Where Unit 481 definitions in src/**/*.test.ts Counted by grep at the 24 October snapshot Validation 25 definitions in 9 files src/**/*.validation.ts Browser (Playwright) 27 definitions in 2 files: 22 desktop, 5 mobile e2e/app.spec.ts, e2e/mobile.spec.ts The grep counts it( and test( at the start of a line, so parametrised and template-generated tests are undercounted. The Playwright config defines desktop Chromium at 1440 by 900, a Pixel 7 profile and an iPhone 14 viewport, so each browser test can run several times. Figures The overview-light, overview-dark and rogue-wave captures below were made for this portfolio and predate the 9–24 October 2026 render and scenery merges. They show the interface at that point, not the current deployed build. Light theme overview with a moderate sea and a container ship. Dark theme hurricane preset with a tanker and a carrier. Rogue wave preset following a container ship. Underwater camera looking up at 4.0 m. Underwater view of a hull at 6.1 m. Clear oceanic water at 3.9 m. Turbid coastal water, Jerlov type 9, at 3.7 m. HDR bloom on. HDR bloom off. Reproducibility pnpm install pnpm dev # http://localhost:5173 pnpm test # unit tests pnpm validate # longer statistical physics validation pnpm build && pnpm test:e2e # browser tests on desktop and phone viewports pnpm check # format, lint, typecheck, unit tests and build Experiments are deterministic: the same saved file produces the same sea, because amplitudes are seeded per cell with a counter-based hash and the physics advances in exact fixed steps. Tools are pinned in package.json and pnpm-lock.yaml: for example Three.js ~0.186.1, Playwright 1.56.1 and TypeScript 5.9.3. The package manager is pnpm 10.28.0. The live demo is the production build committed to docs/ on main by pnpm deploy:pages and served by GitHub Pages from a branch. There are no GitHub Actions workflows. The build uses relative asset paths, so it runs from any static host. Engineering quality Types and lint. Strict TypeScript, ESLint with jsx-a11y and Prettier. Accessibility. Axe-core runs with WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 A and AA tags on the desktop app, in both themes and with a dialog open, and on phone viewports. The 3D view is keyboard operable, and everything it shows is also available as text. Colour tokens meet AA contrast in both themes. Phones. Below 900 px the scene, inspector and dock share one cell; the browser tests check no horizontal overflow, touch editing and the More menu on a Pixel 7 and an iPhone 14 in both orientations. Touch targets are at least 44 px on touch devices, with one exemption: the camera and overlay controls drawn on top of the 3D view stay shorter (32 px in the stylesheet) so they do not cover the sea. Range sliders are 36 px. Contracts. Plain TypeScript interfaces separate vessels, renderer and simulation. Robustness. A lost WebGL context is rebuilt, and phones and software renderers use a coarser mesh. Limitations and next steps What the physics note says is not modelled or is simplified: Current: no refraction by current gradients, no shear with depth, no wave steepening against an opposing current. The inspector warns when an opposing current exceeds half the peak group velocity, and again past blocking. Flooding: no sloshing dynamics, no cross-flooding time, 100 per cent permeability, floodwater adds weight but not inertia, one lumped breach per compartment. Moorings: quasi-static line with no snap loads, frictionless flat seabed, anchor holding independent of line angle. Waves: the Stokes second-order term is capped, and the shallow-water regime beyond Stokes validity is not covered. The fourth cascade is visual only, and the GPU draws a subset of the CPU fields. Weather: gusts and squalls act on vessels and the picture, not on the wave spectrum. Lightning is visual only. The hull model is strip theory at the lowest fidelity tier, not a panel or CFD code. Underwater optics are for rendering and do not feed the physics. Plan versus shipped The master plan (last updated 2026-10-02) proposed raw WebGPU. The shipped renderer uses WebGL 2 through Three.js, because every current browser supports it and the renderer is isolated behind an interface so a WebGPU backend could follow. The plan also had vessels read the GPU surface back. The shipped design samples a CPU evaluation of the same spectral components in the worker, which keeps physics deterministic and testable in Node. The plan’s later phases are not built: Stokes and cnoidal waves, grid shallow-water and Boussinesq solvers, a scripting API, and higher-fidelity radiation. The plan also describes a “Reference” CPU float64 mode that I have not verified as shipped.

d: A real-time 3D ocean-wave and ship-motion sandbox that runs in the browser, built on published wave spectra and checked against analytic results.
h: At a glance The problem Approach What I built Results What I learned Stack
b: Wave Laboratory Side project · simulation & graphics Launch the lab The lab needs a browser with WebGL 2. It runs on desktop and on phones. At a glance 4 FFT cascades, from 1 km swells down to centimetre ripples 280 water columns, at most, sampled under a hull to integrate pressure 481 + 25 unit and validation test declarations at the 24 October 2026 snapshot, counted by grep; not a current passing-test count The problem I have always liked how much of the sea can be written as a short recipe. A real ocean is not one wave. It is thousands of simple waves of different lengths and directions added together, and oceanographers describe how much energy each one carries with a curve called a spectrum. Ships respond to that sum, not to any single wave. I wanted a place to build a sea from those published recipes, drop ships into it, and watch and measure what happens, with the physics honest enough that the numbers mean something and the page still running smoothly in a browser tab. Approach Wave Laboratory architecture: a validated experiment file drives a Zustand store and React UI; SimClient exchanges messages with a simulation worker, one request at a time; the WebGL2 renderer inverse-transforms the same wave amplitudes on the GPU and checks them against the CPU. The sea is built from named, published models. The energy curve comes from JONSWAP, Pierson–Moskowitz or Bretschneider spectra, with a depth correction (TMA) for shallow water and Hasselmann’s fetch-limited growth for seas built by wind. Waves are spread over directions, and the speed of each wave follows the dispersion relation, including water depth and surface tension. The surface is then synthesised with an inverse FFT on four grids of different sizes, with a “choppy” sideways displacement that sharpens crests. Ships float by pressure integration: for each moment, the simulation sums the water pressure over the part of the hull that is underwater (buoyancy plus the Froude–Krylov wave force), then adds added mass, damping, propulsion, rudder and wind. A freak wave can be placed on purpose using NewWave theory, which lines up many components so their crests meet at one point and time. The Draupner crest, 18.5 m in a sea with a significant height of 11.9 m, is the reference case. What I built Deterministic simulation. The same experiment file always produces the same sea. Physics runs at a fixed time step in a Web Worker, and the main thread keeps at most one request in flight, so a slow machine runs slower than real time rather than building a queue. What you see is what the ships feel. The GPU draws the sea from the same amplitudes the CPU physics uses. On each new sea it compares one texel with the CPU result and logs an error if they disagree. The browser tests fail if that error appears. Instruments. Wave gauges, ship motion recorders, power spectra by Welch’s method, wave statistics, motion-sickness incidence and CSV export. Underwater view. Light fades per colour with depth for the chosen Jerlov water type, and the surface seen from below shows Snell’s window. Weather, damage and moorings. Gusts, squalls, rain and fog; flooding compartments; anchor chains modelled as elastic catenaries. Phones and accessibility. A phone layout with panel switching and touch targets of at least 44 px, except the camera controls drawn on top of the 3D view, which stay shorter so they do not cover the sea (the stylesheet sets them to 32 px). It also has light and dark themes, keyboard operation and WCAG 2.2 AA contrast. Accessibility is checked with axe in the browser tests on desktop and phone-sized viewports. Results The lab with its default moderate sea: a container ship under way, with scene tree, sea-state readout and instrument dock. The rogue-wave preset: a container ship in a storm sea, with a focused NewWave crest due at a gauge 380 m ahead. The lab at sunset: a container ship in a Beaufort 6 sea, HDR bloom on. The same view with bloom off. Underwater camera at 6.1 m, looking at a hull from below. Turbid coastal water (Jerlov type 9) at 3.7 m: blue light is absorbed first, so the view is dark green. Heads up. This is a teaching and exploration tool, not a certified seakeeping program. The reference notes list what is not modelled, such as current shear with depth, wave refraction by currents, and floodwater sloshing. The technical report covers these limits. What I learned Putting the sea’s recipe in one place, then reading it from both the CPU and the GPU, made disagreements easy to find and fix. A test that fails when the two sides disagree is worth more than careful reading. Writing down what a model does not cover, and warning the user when they leave its range, is part of the physics. Accessibility checks in the browser tests caught issues I would not have found by eye. Stack TypeScript React Three.js WebGL 2 Web Workers Zod Zustand Vite Vitest Playwright axe-core
